subtopic: COAL EXPORTS FROM BRITISH COLUMBIA-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I move an urgent and pressing motion under Standing Order 43 with regard to a deal entered into between the Government of Canada and the Soviet Union to provide a low interest loan of $180 million so as to facilitate the production and expedition of Siberian coal to world markets. Having regard to the real difficulties experienced by coal producers and provincial governments in western Canada in putting in place the necessary infrastructure to enable coal from northeast British Columbia to compete with the coal from Siberia in world markets, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley (Mr. McCuish):
That the government, through the Minister of Transport, immediately reopen negotiations with British Columbia offering no less than the same terms of financing negotiated with the Soviet Union to put in place the rail and port facilities which would facilitate the shipment of northeast coal to world markets.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under Standing Order 43. Whereas U.S. coals used in acid rain areas in Ontario contain 5 per cent or more sulphur content, and whereas Lethbridge coal and East Coulee coal contain only .05 per cent or less sulphur content, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker):

subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF PROGRAM IN WINDSOR, ONT.-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 concerning the application of the unemployment insurance program in the Windsor area. Considering that unemployment is currently running at 13.7 per cent of the work force, as recorded by Statistics Canada, yet the Department of Manpower and Immigration continues to use an unemployment figure of 11.3 per cent which results in a greater hardship on workers applying for unemployment insurance benefits, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy):
That this House instruct the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Agriculture, all of whom represent the hard working people of Windsor, to take time from their other grandiose activities and remember their responsibilities to the people of the Windsor area, and to meet with their colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, to straighten out the administration of the unemployment insurance benefits in the Windsor area.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I move as follows. Whereas the economic slump occasioned by the ill-conceived Liberal budget of October 28 has driven the Canadian dollar below 84 cents U.S., accompanied yesterday by tailspin losses on stock markets across Canada in the wake of the prospects

November 25, 1980
of yet even higher interest rates, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott):
That credible measures be taken to stabilize Canadian interest rates at a level consistent with sustained economic growth, rather than blindly following the Liberal policy of high and accelerating interest rates necessitated by the government's utter failure to combat inflation.

MEASURES TO IMPROVE PRODUCTIVITY AND INVESTMENT-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to move a motion under Standing Order 43. Since October 28, 1980, the Canadian dollar has continued to slide, slide and slide, despite the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spent 12 days in his Middle East tour courting wealth and oil and whatever else in the Arab world. Yesterday the dollar closed at below 84 cents, the lowest level for a considerable time. The projections concerning inflation were based on the dollar being 86 cents during 1980, 87.5 cents during 1981 and 88 cents during 1982. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That the government introduce new measures forthwith to improve productivity and the investment, climate in Canada so as to restore confidence in our currency.

CALL FOR IMPLEMENTATION OF POLICY OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. This morning the Canadian Institute for Economic Policy-not exactly an NDP think tank-released a study called the "Energy Squeeze", which foresees an energy shortfall within the next 20 years. In Bruce Wilson's opening statement, he slams the national energy policy and says, first, that the program does not refute the myth that energy self-sufficiency can be achieved simply by raising prices; second, that as a consequence of such arbitrary price increases the level of foreign ownership in the Canadian economy will grow substantially-not go down; and third, that the program is highly inflationary, offering substantial price increases for domestic oil and gas production, thereby creating huge and unnecessary financial windfalls relative to today's known reserves, such windfalls to be paid by and for the Canadian consumer.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson):
That this government immediately implement the New Democratic Party energy policy by taking under public ownership Imperial Oil, Shell and Texaco; and secondly, that the federal government begin an industrial strategy or an industrial restructuring in this country that this report indicates is badly needed.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The Wheat Board is currently offering number one red spring wheat for sale at prices in excess of $7 and durum for $9 per bushel, and the initial payment to farmers is only $4.25 and $5 respectively. So far in the current crop year the Wheat Board has sold almost three-quarters of a million tonnes more than it has accepted in deliveries from farmers. The resulting reduction in inventory means that the Canadian Wheat Board is unfairly holding considerable moneys that belong to farmers. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone):
November 25, 1980

That the government immediately instruct the Canadian Wheat Board to increase the initial payments for spring wheat by $1.50 per bushel and for durum wheat by $2 per bushel.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO VICTIMS OF ITALIAN EARTHQUAKE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs. Yesterday this House unanimously urged the minister to consult with the Italian government in order to consider ways in which we might provide special and immediate help to the victims of the devastating earthquake in the Naples-Saler-no area of southern Italy. Can the minister tell us whether he has consulted with the Italian government and whether in fact there is some plan to bring forward an aid program greater than the one described yesterday to the hon. member for Saint-Denis.

speechtext: Perhaps I could repeat the question for the minister, Madam Speaker. Madam Speaker, I spoke twice this morning with the Italian ambassador. In between times he communicated with

his government in Rome. I have also communicated with the Italian-Canadian committee, which is about to raise funds to assist the earthquake victims in Italy. I believe the sum of $100,000, which I announced yesterday, has already been transmitted by the Canadian Red Cross to the Italian Red Cross. subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO VICTIMS OF ITALIAN EARTHQUAKE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the minister will know full well that the motion yesterday outlined a number of other matters that might be regarded by him as appropriate. However, could we have a commitment from the minister that he will make a statement on motions outlining the total plan of relief which is proposed, preferably today but, if not, tomorrow, specifically with regard to the other matters raised in the motion?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO VICTIMS OF ITALIAN EARTHQUAKE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 will certainly give a commitment to the House that in one form or another I will make the plan public. However, I suspect that tomorrow will be too soon. Unfortunately, the Italians are still discovering new dimensions to this great catastrophe and the dreadful death toll is still mounting. It will be some days before the full extent of the tragedy is known and the kind of assistance that we might give can appropriately be decided.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO VICTIMS OF ITALIAN EARTHQUAKE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I wish to refer specifically to one matter raised in the motion. I think we all know that as the tragedy unfolds the numbers coming in climb higher and higher each day. I appreciate the minister's dilemma on that. However, last year as the government we gave consideration to and introduced a program of airlifts to the earthquake victims in the Azores. A community in Canada was trying to help them and regarded the airlift program as particularly useful in making sure that the necessary aid got there. Yesterday the minister said that he would prefer not to use such a program. Can we have from him a statement today that he will reconsider his commitment yesterday to help only with cash? As well, can he give some undertaking that the airlift program which was used last year will also be used in this program?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO VICTIMS OF ITALIAN EARTHQUAKE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it may be that there will be the need for an airlift program if certain medical supplies or eventually building supplies have to be sent to Italy from Canada.
I might reiterate the point 1 made yesterday-and I might say that the Italian government feels this very strongly as well-that it will not be very useful, especially in the early days, if people in Canada start collecting goods to send to Italy. What they need is money. That is the view of the Italian government as well as of this government.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is also for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The minister will know of large gatherings of Italian-Canadians in Toronto and Hamilton last night and the very real emotion expressed in those cities which will be reflected in Italian-Canadian communities across the country. The minister said he had been in touch with the Italian-Canadian committee. Is the government planning to be in touch with other organizations such as the Italian congress? Did the government have a representative at either of the meetings in Hamilton or Toronto last night? In any event, since the motion stipulates that the government consult with the many Canadians who are able and willing to render assistance, how will the minister consult with the many concerned people in this country in the days ahead?

speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is always a difficult question to know how to consult a body of citizens in our country which has a number of different representative organizations. What assurances can the Secretary of State for External Affairs give those Canadians who wish to respond in an urgent and generous manner that their donations will get to where they are intended and where we all would wish.

I am told that although suspicions were raised with respect to the previous catastrophe in Italy, the considered judgment now is that all the money was well dispensed. NORTH-SOUTH RELATIONS REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING RESTRUCTURING OF ECONOMIC INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
My
question is for the Prime Minister. Welcome.

subtopic: NORTH-SOUTH RELATIONS REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING RESTRUCTURING OF ECONOMIC INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: NORTH-SOUTH RELATIONS REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING RESTRUCTURING OF ECONOMIC INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
In light of the Prime Minister's sudden interest in addressing North-South issues and in light of his remarks in Paris yesterday that he would like to see a change
November 25, 1980

in emphasis from traditional development assistance to a restructuring of international economic and other institutions, will he tell the House whether his government is now planning to give detailed attention to tariffs, industrial conversion, International Monetary Fund rules and other national and international economic restructuring measures?

subtopic: NORTH-SOUTH RELATIONS REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING RESTRUCTURING OF ECONOMIC INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: Dance around that one, Pierre.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: NORTH-SOUTH RELATIONS REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING RESTRUCTURING OF ECONOMIC INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
1 am afraid I do not have an answer to that one, Pierre. I have been discussing this subject for a few years now, notwithstanding what the hon. lady says. I refer to a speech 1 made at Mansion House when 1 became a freeman of the city of London some three or four years ago.
This is not a new idea and I am not the originator of it. I think it is a matter for all of us to understand that the debate between the North and South is more a question of power sharing than the solving of any particular problem, either by way of aid or changes in tariff structures such as the hon. lady refers to. Tariffs and quotas are something, of course, that have been discussed at the summits which 1 have attended. They have been the object of decisions by this government and other governments and are constantly under review with the intention of keeping in balance the need to adjust our economies and prevent too great rises of unemployment at a given time, at the same time respecting the Third World countries' desire to gain increasing markets in the developed world.
These are not matters I can discuss in an answer during question period but 1 would be happy to participate in any debate that the opposition parties would want to have on perhaps one of the opposition days.

subtopic: NORTH-SOUTH RELATIONS REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING RESTRUCTURING OF ECONOMIC INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: The Prime Minister says this is not a matter for the question period, yet it was a matter for a press conference in Paris where he explicitly stated that he would like to see a de-emphasis on development assistance and a greater emphasis on restructuring economic institutions. Therefore, I would like to know what the government is definitely planning to do, since that was a clear question at the press conference. In that connection, could 1 ask the Prime Minister whether or not he is aware the Secretary of State for External Affairs said publicly last week that he had told cabinet that "unless we increase official development aid we will be under increased pressure to move on other points" to redress the North-South situation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: NORTH-SOUTH RELATIONS REMARKS OF PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING RESTRUCTURING OF ECONOMIC INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member said that it was the subject of a press conference. It was a question which was asked of me and which I attempted to answer in good faith, as I am attempting to answer her questions. I did not plan then and do not plan today to review in detail the many measures that this government is preparing for. We hope to make a presentation at the summit in Ottawa next July. My aim at this stage is not to convince the hon. lady that we are doing well; it is to try to ensure that the seven participants of
Ora! Questions
that summit in July will be able to make some progress, particularly in this year of economic difficulties for all countries. I am attempting to study a range of measures with the participants so that we can reach agreement on some of them.
In so far as the quote of the Secretary of State for External Affairs is concerned, I see nothing objectionable to that. We have stated through his mouth and through the voice of the Minister of Finance that we want to have increased developmental assistance. That does not mean that in other areas we cannot make progress, but it does mean that we must act on both fronts at the same time.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING MEASURES TO STIMULATE ACTIVITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for Sheik Yamani's dancing partner, the "Astaire of Arabia", the Prime Minister. While the Prime Minister was away dealing with world problems, the cost of living figures in Canada rose 10.9 per cent year over year. Interest rates have increased in the Bank of Canada and the prime rates of the banks increased to 13% per cent. The Canadian dollar is down to its lowest point since February, 1979. In Ontario they had to bring in a mini-budget to compensate for the lack of economic stimulus in the federal budget. Imperial Oil cancelled their $8 billion Cold Lake heavy oil project.
My question to the Prime Minister is this. When he came back from the Bonn summit, he introduced a new program of government expenditure reduction to deal with these similar economic problems. Now that he is back from the Saudi summit, what does he propose to do about these extremely severe economic and financial problems that we are suffering from in this country, and when will he make an announcement about these?

November 25, 1980
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of State, Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
subsubtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING MEASURES TO STIMULATE ACTIVITY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the government was aware of the figures provided by the hon. member with respect to the unemployment rate as well as other economic indicators when it prepared the budget. The Minister of Finance has laid down in his budget a scenario for the economic recovery of Canada. He has taken responsible tax measures that avoid the pitfall of trying to come out too hastily from a recession and, at the same time, avoid fleecing the most deprived in our society in an attempt to control inflation. The budget is laying down the scenario for an economic recovery and we will see its results in the very near future.

speakerposition: subtopic

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is addressed to the Prime Minister, if he can get his head out of the sand. While he has been away, 36 acting prime ministers have been answering. Now that the Prime Minister is back the Canadian people expect some answers from him. They would sooner have him waltzing with Premier Lougheed than doing the moozmaad with Sheik Yamani.
While the Prime Minister was away, the Minister of Finance said that Canadians will have to accept a lower standard of living to adjust to higher energy prices. As a matter of fact, personal disposable income has dropped severely this year in real terms. Does the Prime Minister support the view of the Minister of Finance that Canadians now have to accept a lower standard of living and adjust to these higher energy prices, or does he disagree? If he agrees with the Minister of Finance, what action is he going to take so that Canadians do not have to accept a lower standard of living? When is he going to worry about the standard of living of Canadians?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I apologize to the hon. member. It takes a moment to adjust to his vulgarity after having been associated with-
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
I have not seen the statement attributed to the Minister of Finance. It is certain that with the very rapid rise in prices of imported petroleum there has been a transfer of real wealth from the industrialized societies to the OPEC countries. This has resulted in Canada and every other oilimporting nation having a slower growth of real income. There are some years in which certain sectors of society have even seen a standstill and a slight recession, but by and large the hon. member knows that real wealth is still growing in Canada in average terms for Canadians, and it will continue, except that I think Canadians must accept that it cannot continue to
grow as rapidly as it did before the OPEC nations caused this very large and rapid increase in oil prices.

Madam Speaker, it may be vulgar to ask the Prime Minister questions about these annoying economic problems in Canada, but the Canadian people do not think it is vulgar. They want some answers.
I bring to the attention of the Prime Minister that in the battle to overcome regional disparity there has just been a report from the Economic Council of Canada that in Newfoundland, after all these years of attempts by the Prime Minister and others to overcome regional disparity, unemployment insurance is one-twelfth of the total personal income of the people of Newfoundland compared with one-fortieth in Canada. The House resumed from Monday, November 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Waddell:
That the proclamation laid before the House on Wednesday, November 12, 1980, pursuant to subsection 35(2) of the Petroleum Administration Act, as proclaimed in PC 1980-2915, be revoked.

Madam Speaker, when the House adjourned last night, I was saying that the basic issue regulating oil pricing and distributing revenues among the producer provinces, the federal government and the industry was whether there would be in the future a federal government with the means to protect the interests of all Canadians.
I also said that I had had an analysis made of the financial situation of the federal government in relation to that of the provincial governments. The large increase in the federal deficit during the last five years, in spite of serious efforts to limit expenditures, has reduced the freedom of action of the federal government to stimulate the economy and implement new programs. The situation of the provinces is so complex that the revenue structure varies for each of them and that some have a deficit while others have a surplus. Mr. Speaker, it is very obvious that if we compare both situations, the deficit of the federal government and the percentage of the budget

November 25, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act
that the government must use to pay debt charges are much larger than those of the provinces.
For instance, in 1974, federal revenues were $29,600 million. In 1979, they were $42,554 million. The expenditures in 1974 amounted to $27,895 million. In 1979, they amounted to $51,320 million. In 1974, the federal government had a surplus of $1.1 billion, but in 1979, it had a deficit of $9.1 billion. On the other hand, debt charges in 1974 amounted to $2.9 billion, or 10.6 per cent of total expenditures, but in 1979, they made up 15.8 per cent of federal expenditures, or $8 billion.
Mr. Speaker, when we compare this situation with that of all the provincial governments combined-because this is what we have to do when we are talking about the relationship between the financial position of the provinces and that of the federal government-this is what we find. Let us look at the combined revenues of the provincial governments for 1974. They amounted to $25,315 million. In 1979, they totalled $49,522 million. In 1974, their expenditures amounted to $23,372 million, and in 1979, to $47,234 million.
In 1974, the provinces as a whole had a surplus of $652 million. In 1979, they still had a surplus of $553 million. The debt service charge for all the provinces in 1974 was $1,545 million, and in 1979, $3,399 million, or almost $3.4 billion. Their surplus, and not a deficit, as in the case of the federal government, amounted to 2.8 per cent of their expenditures in 1974 and remained at 1.2 per cent in 1979.
If we compare, Mr. Speaker, the financial position of the federal government, either surplus or deficit, with that of the provincial governments, we note the difference. In 1979, the federal deficit amounted to 17.9 per cent of federal spending, the debt service charge made up 15.8 per cent of federal spending, while for all the provinces, with a 1.2 per cent surplus over their expenditures, the debt service charge represented only 7.2 per cent of their spending. And this, Mr. Speaker, even when we consider that the provincial governments did not have to stimulate the Canadian economy as the federal government had to do, especially since 1974.
Another table that was drawn up for me shows that the federal government has provided a great number of incentives since 1974: minimum income tax reduction upped from $150 to $200 in November, 1974; and increased again in June, 1975, for a cost to the federal treasury of $610 million; deduction on retirement income, extension of the $1,000 deduction on interest revenue in the budget of November,
1974,	cost to the federal treasury: $135 million; federal sales tax on building materials brought down to 5 per cent in November, 1974, for a cost of $600 million; exemption from the federal sales tax of transportation materials, $150 million; investment tax credit provided in the federal budgets of June,
1975,	and March, 1977, another $430 million to stimulate the economy; child tax credit in March, 1977, $275 million;
increase in the employment expense deduction in March, 1977, $120 million; tax break for business stocks, $350 million; increase in the basic personal income tax deduction for 1978 in the October, 1977, budget, $700 million; federal compensation for cutbacks in provincial sales tax in April, 1978, $760 million.
We can see therefore, Mr. Speaker, that since 1974 it is the federal government which has had to increase its expenditures or to stabilize them in certain sectors in order to reduce taxes or increase expenditures on a selective basis as an incentive for job creation. The figures I have given are the result of these measures. The federal government finds itself in a position where the deficit is at the 17.9 per cent level and 15.8 per cent of our spending is used to service the federal debt.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, as I said last night, those who claim that the budget is not generous toward the producing provinces must be made to show how we are not being generous. I said last night that as a result of this budget Alberta would be getting over $31 billion within four years. Yet members opposite claim that is not enough. Obviously I would have preferred that an agreement be reached instead of having to proclaim provisions under the Petroleum Administration Act, which the government had no choice but to proclaim on November 12. I wish this could be settled amicably, I wish we could have a written agreement. But failing this, Mr. Speaker, I feel there is a clear duty, the responsibility imparted by this Parliament in the legislation enacted six years ago, to ensure that we have in Canada a system of oil and natural gas prices established in the interest of all Canadians. As I said, energy is the most important factor in the future development of our economy. Indeed, it will shape our future society. We will have to adjust to these new realities. How can we as members of this Parliament that must represent all of Canada, say that we want that direction to be followed in the interest of all Canadians, if the federal treasury does not have a major share of the oil and gas revenues to guarantee this?
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I submit that all hon. members should decide once and for all whether we are going to have a government that will be able to deal with all those issues, or a federal government that will be at the mercy of some provinces. I explained earlier the financial situation of the provinces as a whole, but I could give the financial status of the oil producing provinces, because this shows in a better light still the fact that the Canadian government is not in a position to govern. Alberta's revenues were $2.7 billion in 1974, but they topped $6 billion in 1978. In 1974, that province had a surplus amounting to 34.2 per cent of its expenditures; in 1978, the percentage rose to 40 per cent. Debt service charges fell from 5.1 per cent in 1974 to 3.7 per cent only in 1978. Alberta's surplus in relation to the gross provincial expenditures went from 4.2 per cent in 1974 to 5.9 per cent in 1978. The same goes for Saskatchewan, increases across the board, as well as for British Columbia. Coming eastward, Manitoba is almost in
November 25, 1980

a deficit situation, so are Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland. Who is going to see that the interests of Canadians in all those other provinces are protected? I suggest the situation is much more serious than it has been indicated in the debates, and I am tremendously concerned that nobody looks at those figures. The important point is the percentage of the federal budget that goes to debt service charges.
Because it will keep increasing year after year, the federal government has a responsibility to stimulate the economy in a period of economic slowdown, the provincial governments cannot do it by themselves, only the federal government can. Mr. Speaker, it is obvious the government had the duty to intervene. It is its responsibility. Producing provinces should indeed receive a fair share, as I stated last night. Alberta after all will get $31 billion over a four year period under the proposed formula, Saskatchewan will get $3.2 billion, British Columbia $3.6 billion. So all those hon. members should stop saying that the federal government is unfair and does not take into account the aspirations of the west and should tell me clearly how much more money they would like to be transferred because they are saying that $31 billion is not enough, $3.2 billion to Saskatchewan is not enough, $3.6 billion to B.C. is not enough. They should stop making long speeches and tell me clearly how much more money they would transfer to these provinces and tell me also what is going to happen to the financial situation of the federal government in the coming years if such a solution were retained.
Then they should answer not only to their fellow citizens but also here in the House of Commons and in the rest of Canada, and they should decide whether they want the rest of the people of Canada to have a say in the development of the economy of this country, or else only two, perhaps three provinces, and perhaps from four to five million Canadians out of a population of 23 million, will have a say in the development of the Canadian economy.
Mr. Speaker, this is not the kind of Canada where I learned to live, nor the kind of Canada where I am prepared to work. There will come a time when people will have to decide whether the government will look not only after the Canadian electorate but also after the other provinces 1 have mentioned, which are heading more and more toward deficit positions and where the percentage of expenditures to cover the service of the debt is growing while it is decreasing as far as oil producing provinces and the federal government are concerned. This is a matter we must face clearly, Mr. Speaker, and I think it is time to do so.
I should like to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by quoting some figures to show the difference in the consumer price of a gallon of gas from what was proposed in the Progressive Conservative budget of December, 1979. According to the budget brought forward by the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on October 28, 1980, gas will cost
Petroleum Administration Act
$1.36 a gallon in 1981. Under the Progressive Conservative budget of December 1979, it would have cost $1.56 a gallon or 20 cents more, and those are the people who were attacking us last week and the week before saying we were being too rough with the consumers. Those same people would have increased the price of gas for all Canadian workers and all Canadian producers in 1981 by 20 cents more than we did in the October 28 budget. In 1982, the price will be $1.53 under the Liberal budget and it would have been $1.75 under the Progressive Conservative budget, or 22 cents more a gallon. And it keeps rising. But let us look at the difference for 1983; the price will be $1.71 a gallon under the Liberal budget, but it would have been $2.63 under the Progressive Conservative budget. I see that the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie) is paying close attention to those figures. I know he is concerned about the consumers in the province of New Brunswick. So when his party says that the budget of the Liberal finance minister, the October 28 budget, is not fair to the province of New Brunswick, what can he say to what his government would have done, because in 1984, the difference would be 68 cents more a gallon, or about 50 per cent of what we pay today, if the Progressive Conservatives had remained in power.
Mr. Speaker, I think everyone realizes that we did a great service to Canadians in December by voting against the government, against that budget to make sure the interests of all Canadian consumers would be well protected.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased today to have the opportunity to make some remarks concerning the implementation of an energy policy for Canada. I can see that the ground has been heavily plowed and many of the issues have been covered. I would like to cover four brief aspects that I feel have been left out.
I would like to direct my comments concerning the energy policy to its effect on low and middle-income Canadians. I would also like to comment on the effects, as 1 see them, on a Canadian industrial strategy, and on aboriginal people in Canada. Finally, I will have a question at the end: does this energy policy establish a greater sense of community within Canada?
If I could just briefly address these four points, 1 will proceed first with the question of how the energy policy affects Canadian consumers. I say this without malice. I think the geography of our country militates against certain kinds of distribution occurring. 1 feel that this energy policy, because of the geography of our country, tends to favour central Canada over some of the regions. Basically, it favours urban Canada over rural Canada and some of the remote outposts. I will come to some of these matters in a few moments.
One of the most objectionable features of this energy policy is that it contains very strong privileges for foreign-owned oil companies in Canada. These privileges are given at the expense of low and middle-income Canadians. A few figures
i

November 25, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act
might help. In 1979 the oil industry should have paid $5.1 billion in tax at the official rate of 36 per cent for corporate tax. It only paid $1.4 billion. Since 1974 the industry has paid tax at the effective rate of only 10 per cent. This is due to the generous tax concessions given to these oil companies in return for something we expected.
When the question was put to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) as to why we were charging the consumers in Canada, placing the whole burden of this program on the backs of the consumers, he made a statement which is very interesting. When asked why consumers and not the companies, the minister stated, "We felt it was not appropriate to go higher than we have in the budget on the industry. We still want to leave that industry with large incentives to go ahead and make money." Frankly, that answer is not acceptable. They have basically placed the burden of this elaborate program on consumers within Canada, especially on those who can afford it the least. That is unacceptable. Time will tell as this takes its course that it will be unacceptable to the Canadian people.
As we explore this matter further as to the effect on consumers on budget night, October 28, it is interesting to note that a speech by the minister basically recognized in the budgetary projections that this energy policy would increase the consumer price index. It will further erode the income of Canadians. He stated, "Be aware of it and be prepared to live with it." Very shortly thereafter, it was proven that some of those projections were wrong. I suggest the one on the consumer price index was very wrong. Because of the combined effect of the energy policy and the taxation program put in place by the budget, especially on the cost of energy, those projections on the consumer price index were in error and will be much higher.
Before we examine what this consumer price index or erosion of real income will be, we have to look at the total formula being faced by Canadians. Some of this energy policy will result in an erosion of wealth in some areas of this country. Municipalities will have to increase taxes. That is happening already. Provincial governments will increase taxes and cut services. That is happening. It will not mean a direct tax imposition such as income tax where it is theoretically graduated and progressive, with those receiving the greatest benefits paying the most. We are not aiming at that kind of tax. The kind of budget and energy policy we have in place is the most direct regressive tax. Those are the taxes that are emphasized. I suggest that those are the taxes that will hit low and middle-income Canadians, making them foot the bill.
Basically that combined formula of very direct regressive taxation, dramatically high energy costs and the government's policy of interest rates, as has been stated many times in this House, is an eighteenth century monetarist policy. Interest rates on mortgages are around 15 per cent or 15'/2 per cent. We are looking at small business loans crawling back up to the all time high of 19 per cent. These are passed directly through to consumers, to low and middle-income Canadians. We therefore have that combined formula that we have to examine. The
energy policy, rather than in any way alleviating the dramatic rising costs to low and middle-income Canadians, is accelerating them. Frankly, my party believes that is unacceptable. So did the government strangely enough, but something has gone haywire.
In the Speech from the Throne the government committed itself to protect Canadians who are least able to pay. We saw that commitment in writing. It recognized that there must be a fight against inflation. It recognized that energy prices were going to go up and there would have to be some dramatic new developments in the energy sector. It stated that low and middle-income Canadians should not have to bear the burden squarely on their backs. But, lo and behold, there is nothing in the budget, there is nothing here. The government clearly failed the consumers of Canada. Its answer to this failure was a $35 increase in the old age security, and some indexing of pensions in Canada. I would submit that these are clearly inadequate and, in fact, will do nothing to mitigate the very serious situation in which these people find themselves.
What the government is doing, Mr. Speaker, is asking low and middle-income Canadians, the consumers, to pay the costs of buying out the oil companies. It is asking the consumers to pay the cost of building pipelines, to pay the cost of tertiary recovery programs and refinery upgrading. It is asking low and middle-income Canadians to pay a tremendous cost to build new oil sands recovery plants, to pay the costs of offshore and frontier exploration, and to provide the funds for the new technology.
They are going to give them the control.

This should not fall on low and middle-income Canadians. It should clearly be undertaken by private enterprise, where costs will be held in line, where in fact the returns will come directly back to Canadians.
Right on!
It should be undertaken by public enterprise-
Oh, oh!
-where costs are low-

It is no Freudian slip, Mr. Speaker. Secondly, on this particular item, it should be paid for by a progressive tax system. I would have the other members in this House rail at that provision, that the progressive tax system in this country does not exist, where people who receive the most should pay the most in funding these very expensive programs. I suggest that the banks and oil companies might lead the way.
Foreign oil companies account for about 77 per cent of petroleum production in this country, and they receive about 82 per cent of all the revenue. These are not Canadian-owned oil companies or public sector companies. Some 82 per cent of
November 25, 1980

the revenue which accrued from our resource wound up in the hands of foreign-owned corporations. That is unacceptable. We are asking the consumers of Canada to pay for this, and at the same time we are giving a bonus like that to foreign-owned oil companies.
In 1979 the oil industry profits after taxes increased by 53.6 per cent, to $4.6 billion. That would go a long way toward funding and driving those important projects in the hands of Canadians. In the first nine months of this year the five major oil companies increased their profits by an average of 65 per cent over the same period in 1979, so it is not a problem. That sector is doing very well at the expense of Canadians, and particularly at the expense of low and middle-income Canadians who are being asked to foot the bill. Clearly, the oil companies should finance the Canadianization of the industry.
We want to see a minimum of three oil firms under public control, and I suggest that the ones to take over are Imperial, Texaco, and Shell. Let us start with the blackmailers and work from there. However, they should be funding that takeover. They are the ones who have been gleaning tremendous revenues from this country, and following their own objectives rather than those of Canadians. In the final analysis, as prices and costs rise, there must be an indexed tax credit. If we are going to see this energy program develop, there should be a tax credit to protect low and middle-income Canadians. This was promised. Protection was promised, and it should be delivered. That is the only fair way to ensure that it is delivered to the people who need it most.
The second thing about this new industrial strategy, this budget, this over-all look, is that it lacks one thing. It is out of phase. First, it is very timid. In the second place it will probably not work. However, finally we must have an industrial strategy with it. We in this country have no concept of where this government is taking us.
We should base an industrial strategy on three points. We could use resource income from resource development to ensure that all Canadians derive the benefits of the resource. The new technology must be developed in Canada by Canadians, and owned by them. Unless that item is under our control we are in very serious difficulty. The second thing in this industrial strategy is that Canada must train a work force of skilled people capable of developing and implementing this new technology in Canada. The final thing is that the development of the resource must be paced. I feel that this is one of the flaws in this energy policy.
We are going into a massive rush to develop our energy resources on all fronts, but if we fail to pace that, Canadian industry across the board will not obtain the full advantage. We need time to implement that program. By using our resources to develop the modern technology with which to build that industry we would wind up with Canadian industries which are relevant to the twenty-first century. We have a Canadian auto industry which is clearly out of date. Our shipbuilding industry is clearly out of date. I and others in my party feel that if we were to pace the development of this particular resource, we would be able to put in place an
Petroleum Administration Act
industrial strategy which would see Canadians with that technology, our work force trained to build and operate the kinds of industries we need and, finally, strong technologically advanced industries which are owned and controlled by Canadians.
Ensuring that we have heavy public involvement, publicly owned enterprise and joint ventures, in my estimation is the only way there will be a responsibility to Canada and a response to the needs of Canadians. This country has a small population spread over a tremendous area. In the past especially in the resource sector we have been prime picking for foreign corporations. I think that Canada's accountability and responsibility could be enhanced if we placed our industrial strategy firmly on the side of publicly-owned enterprises and on joint ventures. We need that presence. If we develop our own resources by these criteria, then this country and its people will never again be subject to the corporate blackmail we have seen in the past, and see today.
I would like to outline for the record the types of corporate blackmail we have seen in the last little while. The government proposes a 50 per cent ownership objective. That is not enough, and it is meaningless. With the techniques of circumventing Canadian control we will not achieve the goal of placing ownership and control in Canadian hands.
Dome Petroleum has made statements that it will pull up its stakes if it cannot get sufficient tax incentives. Dome has pulled in about $411 million in profits in the past three years. It is now aiming for higher profits by charging the highest possible prices. It proposes to sell Canadian gas to Japan, and I do see a statement by the government that it intends to protect Canadian resources for future generations. We are still playing with the export of Canadian energy resources. At any rate, increased ownership in non-energy companies is an example of where the profits which are being earned are being used to broaden the base of these corporations and not to fulfil the task which they were originally developed to serve.
There is a major $100 million exploration program in the United States. If we are giving those kinds of incentives to Dome Petroleum and other Canadian companies, why are they exploring in the United States with our money? Quite frankly, that is completely unacceptable, and it amounts to corporate blackmail. If we were to develop a solid energy policy, and an industrial strategy which is effective, those companies, funded by Canadian tax dollars, would be operating to meet Canadian goals and not away drilling in the United States and threatening, through blackmail, a corporate withdrawal from this country.
On Tuesday, November 18, Imperial announced that it had abandoned the Alberta tar sands because it could not get its way. The Liberals forked over $40 million in taxpayers' money in order to meet Imperial's profit priorities.
The $40 million mark.

Imperial's profits in 1978-this Exxon-owned corporation-were roughly $314 million. In 1979 they were
5048

November 25, 1980
