$493 million. In 1980 they will probably pull in $750 million in profit, and now it is pulling out of the oil sands. That again is an example of corporate blackmail.
On Thursday, November 20, Shell Oil threatened to pull $205 million of investment out of its tar sands project unless it got another $40 million from the mark. We should tell them flatly just to get out, that Petro-Canada will build those tar sands plants, and that if they get out of there they will be getting out of other sectors.
The energy policy which was put forward by the government was supposed to be a change in direction, but in fact it was not. It was a very timid policy, and the actions since it was dropped into this House on October 28 show that the government will continue to provide rich incentives and yield to corporate blackmail. Frankly, this also is not acceptable. They should be told to get out.
On the whole question of an industrial strategy and of how this energy program could develop all of Canadian industry so that Canadians could maximize their benefits from resource development, let me refer to the example of shipbuilding. Pacing the way we develop a resource is important. If this resource is hurled ahead at too fast a pace, the ships required to service and develop the offshore oil and gas industry will have to come from offshore. Foreign countries will build those vessels. We hear talk on the east coast that the liquefied natural gas carriers will be built in Finland. We hear on the west coast that that technology will be developed and put in place in Japan. We hear about sharing and many other things but, nevertheless, those should be built in Canada.
Right on!

We should have and would have had that capability if we had a government committed to this years ago, but it is not just that our supply ships and our liquefied natural gas carriers and the whole offshore marine program will be produced in other areas; if we look at those in this country who are licensed to crew our vessels, we find that the average age of those licensed personnel is 55 years. We need a tremendous influx of trained seamen, and they are not available because this country was not committed to an industrial strategy which took cognizance of that. If we rush the pace of development so quickly that foreign crews will sail foreign-built vessels to move our oil resource, Canadians not only in this generation but also in the next one will fail to receive the maximum benefit.
There is shipbuilding on the west coast, but it is interesting that all the steel comes from Japan. In many other areas the steel comes from Japan. If we are going to expand that industry and all the other component, related or allied industries, we will have to see that steel and other basic commodities come from North America. A Canadian steel plant could provide steel to Canadian shipyards and to the Canadian oil, gas and refining industries based on the west coast, and could provide all of northwest America with a secure supply of steel at reasonable costs. That is absolutely important.
We have the steel in Regina.

There is an absolute absence of an industrial strategy in this country, and it is imperative that one be developed with an energy strategy in order to maximize benefits for Canadians. If that does not happen, we will maximize benefits for those same foreign countries whose economies we have fueled with our resources all during the existence of this country.
The clock is moving along. I mentioned a third item of concern. I want to talk for a moment about the development of energy resources and aboriginal people. The energy program outlined in that entertaining reading brought in on October 28 did take cognizance of native people and their needs. It recognized that many communities in remote areas in which Indian and Inuit people live need an economic boost but, frankly, it mentioned that the bulk of the incentives and the real drives for expansion would be on Canada lands, lands owned and controlled by the Government of Canada.
I think the author of that particular document may have been a little hasty. In fact, a great number of those lands described as Canada lands were in fact Indian and Inuit lands, and still are. As a matter of fact, it is my understanding that this government has a commitment to the rule of law and that basically we do recognize certain claims by aboriginal people to lands and rights within this country. Frankly, I am certain this was an oversight in the document, but we all clearly recognize that when we take something which does not belong to us, that is simply theft.
The last remark which probably should be made is that claims must be acknowledged and dealt with effectively so that native people can share in the abundant resources which exist on the lands claimed by them.
On the positive side-and I might read a little more into the legislation than might be there-in the planning agreements whereby companies go into those lands there will be a requirement to provide training and employment for native people. I commend the authors for that particular aspect. We must create not only a share but also an opportunity to participate. That is a positive aspect.
Does the energy policy-and by its actions this government over the last few months-contribute to establishing a sense of community in the country? Frankly, I really have some serious questions about the energy policy. In my opinion it does not set goals with which Canadians can be identified and work for together, thereby strengthening the sense of community in this country. That does not exist in this energy policy.
Before I move further into that area I would like to go back in Canadian history a little and look at some of the precedents which have brought us to the point at which we are today. In 1979 there was an election, after which a very tired government was retired. The leader of that government crossed this country several times making some very provocative statements. He talked about nuclear energy. He said, "You are going to get it whether you want it or not", in answer to the concerns of many Canadians. He said that farmers were chronic bitchers. He said that if the unemployed wanted work, they should get off their butts. This is not an example of an
November 25, 1980

individual setting and defining goals Canadians can share and work together for, and build a sense of community? But that record goes back to the 1974 election in which, I assume, we all participated. At that time he said, "I promise my government will not impose wage and price controls". In one year he did, and in almost three years it tore the country apart with wage and labour disputes which were artificially created.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext: What does this have to do with the legislation before us?

I will deal with that in just a moment. In 1970, with the stroke of a pen, he eliminated the civil rights of Canadians. I suggest to hon. members opposite, and to others, that this energy policy does not set the goals. It does not establish a sense of community in the country. Basically it opens a wound in some areas.
The hon. member who preceded me stated basically that it was a fair and universally accepted program. But, it is not. Basically it places the hand of the federal government in the pocket of Alberta. It says that certain funds are being removed, but it does not give back the things that are required in return. What will those funds be spent on? Will we get an industrial strategy which will improve the industrial benefits in the west? He says, "No, you will get a $4 billion pork-barrel."
I think there is a tendency to create an enemy in Alberta. I say that with some misgivings, but we must remember that Alberta did not create regional disparity, an inequitable tax system and a $ 15-billion federal deficit for which Albertans to a large degree will pay. This opens a wound in the country, not just for Albertans but for many people who said that the government has failed to live up to the expectations of Canadians. The point now is that the leader of the government has been responsible for it over a decade.
In conclusion, I think Canadians can come together on some of the goals which have been defined. We can re-establish a sense of community, but one of the primary catalysts which will allow this to occur is the resignation of the present leader of the government.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am happy for the opportunity to participate in this debate and hope to bring us back to some sense of reality, especially considering the last few moments and the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly). The hon. member made some of the most remarkable statements I have heard in a while.
Like asking for an industrial strategy; that is remarkable.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Before the member recedes too rapidly, I should like to point out quickly the inconsistency of his saying that the action of the government in relation to the energy package has opened a wound in Alberta, and in the same breath saying that
Petroleum Administration Act
we should nationalize all the oil companies out there. Can one imagine the sort of wound that might open?
Decapitation.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext: That is about what it would amount to. As I listened to the member's remarks on this subject, as well as the remarks of some other members opposite, and as I read the remarks of the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) and of the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) in this debate, I began to feel quite comfortable about this energy package. The reason is that I believe we on this side of the House have every reason to feel confident that we are on the right track when we find the Tories and the NDP attacking us from opposite directions, one saying that we have gone too far and the other saying that we have not gone far enough.
It means you have gone nowhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
It suggests to me that the moderates in the Conservative party and New Democratic Party are really admiring our package while they are trying, as political parties do in elected legislatures, to find some way to disagree with what the administration is doing. Indeed it would be a most unusual debate if members opposite were to come in here and say, "Yes, that is great. We like it all.'There is nothing wrong with it."
If this energy package had been presented to the hon. members of the NDP before its introduction, they would have said that it was great and marvellous. If we look at some of the statements they have made over the past year, then to be consistent they should have come here and said, "Yes, this is a tremendous move, for Petro-Canada to be looking to buy out one of the major multinationals". They should have come in here and praised the 25 per cent land provision as well as the other provisions. But, no, sometimes they are not as intellectually honest as one might wish. They find that they cannot come in here and frankly say, "Yes, that was a tremendous achievement and a great thing for Canada."
Name one member who has been intellectually dishonest.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext: Before turning to the main body of my comments, and aroused by the words of the hon. member for Comox-Powell-
At least name his constituency.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext: I am sorry, the hon. member for Comox-Powell River. In any event, he has a most persuasive and pleasant manner of talking, but he says the most unusual things. He condemned Dome and other private companies. He said that Petro-Canada should take over everything in the country. I want to express my continued basic belief in the mixed economy which is working well for Canada.

It is working well for Dome.

November 25, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext: If Petro-Canada had control over the whole oil industry, it would not be nearly as good a company as it is now.
They would be like the Post Office.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
When we seek to Canadianize the oil industry, I think it is extremely important to see to it that every encouragement is provided not only for great companies like Bob Blair's company, or Dome, but also for all smaller Canadian companies which exist out there and have built up our economy by their incisive approach to business. It is not only important to provide a lot of encouragement to those companies, but also important to provide encouragement and the wherewithal to Petro-Canada.
1 believe there are things which must be done in relation to the rapid expansion of the Canadianization of the oil industry. They must be done by the public sector through Petro-Canada or other federal Crown corporations. But also there is a very important and vital role for the companies that have helped very substantially over the past few years in increasing the amount of Canadian ownership in the country. Petro-Canada has not done it all. The efforts and good leadership of private Canadian oil and gas companies in the west have also made very noteworthy contributions in that regard.
Name two.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I did. Energy represents the geatest challenge to the maintenance of the civilization we have known in our lifetime. We are faced with some very basic facts. The supplies of fossil-based fuels are limited. Throughout the world today there is no subject which involves more time and concern of governments than the question of energy supply, its present price, its future price, and its future supply. Not only are national governments involved in a most intricate manner in this subject throughout the world, but they must be because, if governments are to have the responsibility of managing an economy, then this is the very essence of that responsibility.
It is with that realization, and against that background, that it is necessary to implement the provisions of the Petroleum Administration Act in this country. That step is a very timid one compared to how far governments have gone in relation to this aspect of the economy in other nations of the world.
We have a national responsibility. We have great provincial responsibilities in each of our provinces. We must husband our resources, explore and develop those which are undiscovered, evolve new types of renewable energy making it more feasible and competitive. Of course, we must conserve our resources. While we must prepare for the needs of tomorrow's consumers we must also, at all times, limit the burden to be carried by today's consumers. Therefore the imposition of prices of oil and gas at the national level, to have some consistency from one part of the country to the other, is the essence of national responsibility. I believe that is beyond argument.
In making arguments on this particular motion the opposition will speak about a variety of matters. These are matters which I may say something about. I doubt if any of them are prepared to say seriously that there is not a responsibility of the national government to deal with the question of supply of energy and, at some point, to become affected by the pricing of that energy. After all, it is the setting of price by national governments which has created the entire problem. It is the setting of price by the OPEC cartel that has contributed so substantially to the economic crisis, shall I say, or problems, or malaise, which have characterized the last years of the 1970s. Unfortunately, in doing so in a national government in Canada, responding to what other national governments are doing, there is obviously the question of interference perceived in what had traditionally been an area of price-setting that was not affected directly by the national government. That would be fine, of course, as long as it was not necessary. The unfortunate fact that so much of our oil and gas is concentrated in one area, in one province, tends to make a difficult adversarial conflict between the federal government and the province of Alberta.
I want to express here, as I expressed in Calgary last week to the Calgary Chamber of Commerce, my affection and admiration for the province of Alberta, as a Canadian, and my particular admiration of the incisive approach of their hardworking people and the great contribution they make to Canada. As a maritimer with an inheritance of 100 years of grievances against central Canada, I can, to a considerable degree, sympathize with some of their points of v.iew. I think I have some insight into the reasons those points of view have arisen. Ottawa is the focus of what is referred to as western alienation. But the centralization of industry, of banks and decisions in central Canada is probably more the problem than the question of anything that government does.
If one were to scan my old speeches over the years-and I cannot think of a more tiresome process-you would find they are pretty well filled with illustrations of how centralized we built our economy in this country as compared to other countries. Again and again I have used the example of how American Express can have their corporate headquarters in Phoenix, Arizona, and they find they can serve that country efficiently, whereas in this country, in the business sector, there is too much of a feeling that if you go as far as Oshawa you are in the frontier region.
1 think that in combatting this feeling of alienation in the west not only does government have the responsibility to overcome those feelings, whether they are based on fact or emotion, but in the private sector there needs to be a great deal done in relation to decentralization.
In relation to this debate and the Petroleum Administration Act and its proclamation, I want to say that if I were to summarize quickly what the objectives of a government are in this era in relation to energy, I would have to say that they are as follows: a pricing scheme which lessens the impact on Canadian consumers during the period when there must be escalation in the cost of our energy sources. I think that every
November 25, 1980

member in the chamber will agree that the price of energy will continue to go up, if only because of the fact that new sources of fossil-based fuels tend to be more expensive, in terms of recovery by virtue of their situ, and also because of their diminishing supply. But that does not allow us to forget for a moment that in meeting the other challenges and objectives, which I will talk about later, we cannot forget for a moment that our first obligation is to the Canadian consumer.
Our obligation is to see to it that people can support their families without having such abrupt increases in the cost of something which takes as much of their disposable income as energy, something which rises at a rate that they are simply unable to deal with.
In Canada it is more difficult to adjust to increasing costs of energy abruptly than it is in many other countries. First of all, we live in a northern clime. As a consequence, this means people must heat their homes. There is no way to avoid that. Secondly, we have built our society in such a way, wisely or unwisely, that it is extremely difficult to provide mass transport for very many of our people outside our large cities.
Cars must be used to go to work, to school, to church, and to the stores. In a lot of cases it is ribbon development, but in a lot of other cases it is the free choice that was allowed to be made by Canadian citizens to live in rural settings rather than have all the homes concentrated in an exact village, as has been more the custom in Europe. If you fly over England, France or Germany and you look down you will see a very different pattern than you will see in flying over most of Canada. You see their houses are all very close together and there are very long distances until you come to the next village, where the houses are again concentrated together. One thing about that society is that they do not have to use motorized vehicles as often as we do. In Canada when you look down from a plane you see houses scattered throughout Canada. That is done by choice. Perhaps in relation to transportation it provides an extra problem and penalty for our people today.
I want to make the point that the greatest and most important objective must be not to have an overnight change in price that will deal such a heavy blow to our consumers. Another objective is to achieve a greater share of revenue to meet federal costs. I think in that regard, if you look at what is done in other countries, you will find the share that Canada is taking of the petroleum dollar is smaller than any other country. I will give some figures on that a little later on. Basically, at 10 per cent it was ludicrous; at 24 per cent, which the new arrangement makes-
No, 48 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
-it is substantially below the 37 per cent of the United States and the 48 per cent of Australia, or other countries. Hon. members opposite try to add in other costs to push the percentage upward. That is not accurate at all. It is like saying you should add in the tax that the province charges at the gas pump. That is not right at all. The fact that a government takes part of the energy dollar does not mean that it will not carry out other programs to which it is entitled. The
Petroleum Administration Act
hon. member for Etobicoke Centre did not at all address the question of whether he agrees in principle that the national government of this country, like any other country, has a right to take some portion of that dollar.
I agree.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
He agrees on that. That is progress. Then it becomes a question of degree, and if it is a question of degree, the hon. member will recognize that as the price of energy rises and as energy becomes a larger percentage of the entire economy, the amount which the federal government must take obviously escalates because the increasing cost of energy affects to a very great degree every aspect of the federal operation of providing the basic services of the country. This is a legitimate objective, and I welcome the agreement of the hon. member.
Another objective is a larger share of Canadian ownership in energy.
We agree on that, also.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext: It is obvious that as energy becomes a more important and vital part of our economy it is absolutely essential that the very high degree of American ownership in the oil industry be decreased. I will probably lose the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre when I say that it is also important that there be larger government sector ownership in the oil industry in Canada and that, as a consequence, Petro-Canada should acquire greater holdings than it has at present, and follow the pattern of Mexico, Norway, and elsewhere.
Leave that to the NDP negotiators.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
That is fine because I will stay in the middle, which is a safe place to be. The objectives which I have just mentioned will, unfortunately, incur disagreement with the provinces and the problems of dislocation for industry. The first basic disagreement is whether the OPEC price is a fair world price. As I have said, I visited Alberta last week and people there argue again and again that the OPEC price should be the benchmark price for determining our price. There are few hon. members in this House, as learned as they are, who would, after paying full attention to all aspects of the history of the OPEC price and the actual situation in the world, argue that this is a realistic price. It is a cartel price which is put together by those countries which held a surplus of a commodity which was vital to a purchasing country. The cartel forced up the price by cornering the market and agreeing to a sale price rather than competing in sales. In 1978 and 1979 the price of oil doubled.
There is no doubt that, if this cartel thought it could get away with it, tomorrow it would move up the price to $100 per barrel. I wonder if hon. members opposite would still argue that automatically the Canadian price should relate to the OPEC price, even on a percentage basis, if the price per barrel were moved to $100. The essential, single most telling point

November 25, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act
which must be remembered about that cartel price is that it is the price charged for oil that is surplus to the needs of the countries forming the cartel. Mexico does not charge Mexicans the OPEC price. In Mexico gasoline can be bought for around 40 cents per gallon. Venezuela does not charge Venezuelans the world price, nor does Saudi Arabia charge Saudi Arabians the world price.
What about Australia?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I am talking about the OPEC countries which export oil. Those countries which produce their own oil and which have a surplus to export do not charge the OPEC price for oil and gas to their own people. Why should we in Canada charge that artificial cartel price, or anything like it, to our own people? Surely we can decide in principle that the Canadian price, whatever it should be-and there may be differences-should be based on Canadian conditions and not on some phony comparison to what OPEC happens to be charging this week or next week.
Within the Canadian price there must be incentives for new oil and for frontier oil, as currently being offered by this government. If there are to be incentives, why should we pay the same price for old oil which has been discovered and is simply being pumped out of the ground, when it was profitable at $2.50 per barrel? Why should we push the price of old oil up further to enrich the American companies which own most of those reserves? Every time the price is changed American ownership vastly increases.
That is not so.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
It certainly is so, and I would be very happy to have the hon. member participate in the debate and show me otherwise.
The second disagreement deals with the question of the necessity of increasing the federal take from 10 per cent. I find it shocking that members of the official opposition would side with the government of Alberta on its position. The federal government has taken less of the oil dollar than any government in any federal country, and obviously much less than any government of any unitary country in the world. Yet, as I have said, the percentage of the economy represented by the petroleum industry becomes a larger part of our economy, and the escalating national costs and the program of price equalization require that we have more money. To stay with the ratio of 45/45/10 would be ludicrous in that situation.
I mentioned earlier the figures taken by federal governments in other countries. Again, Australian producers take 37 per cent, the state takes approximately 17 per cent, and the national government takes 48 per cent.
Where is the oil?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext: That applies no matter where the oil is located.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
It will work out to that, as I understand it.
In the United States the producer takes 48 per cent. The great states of Texas, with all the power and authority exercised by Texans in that country, takes only 17 per cent, and the national government takes 35 per cent. 1 suggest that the question of taxes is not of the essence of ownership. The fact that a province or a federal government owns a resource is not the essence of the question of the need or right of either level of government to tax that resource. I am told that in Australia the resource is owned by the state.
It is offshore.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Most of the production is offshore, but that is not the point.
The other point I would like to make is with regard to the large amount taken by Alberta. Hon. members will remember that the government of Alberta took only 22 per cent until 1974. Of course, it receives much more when we include the federal programs. In 1974 the government of Alberta unilaterally changed the figure of .22 per cent and moved it to what works out to be 45 per cent through their involved formula. If the outcry of the industry, that there is an insufficient amount left to the corporations, is correct, it is the government of Alberta which is out of step by the amount which it is taking, not the federal government.
I notice that the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre, the hon. member for Edmonton East, for both of whom I have the greatest respect, and other hon. members, have said that there has been no bargaining in good faith. They said bargaining between the federal government and the provinces was not in good faith. They said the feds did not bargain in good faith. But this second guessing on the negotiation process about who bargained well is not new. All my life I have been accustomed to companies and unions saying that about each other when collective bargaining is under way. The usual expression is that if the other side does not move your way, it means it did not bargain in good faith. I believe that both sides bargained in good faith in this matter. But they have very different responsibilities and a lot at stake. In my opinion, that is the problem.
I am sure the industry feels that government intervention is quite a pain. Industry wonders why it cannot be left alone. But unfortunately if you happen to involve yourself in a business which determines the flow of the entire economy, factors have to be considered that transcend the interests of the company, and even the effect of the policies deemed necessary on the short run level of production or exploration must be considered.
Let us talk about the role of government intervention.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. minister, but the time allotted to him has expired. He may continue with the unanimous consent of the House. Is there unanimous consent?

Agreed.
November 25, 1980

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
My thanks to you, Mr. Speaker, and to hon. members. 1 will try to be as brief as possible. The oil industry, which faces a problem at the present time because of the change in the amount of government take and the new regulations, is an industry which has shown itself over the years to be able to adjust to almost any change one could perceive. For instance, when OPEC took over the ownership of the oil resources a few years ago everyone assumed that this would be an immense problem for the oil industry. Some predicted a breakdown in relation to the way companies operated on an integrated basis, that the majors were ruined because they lost the ownership of these vast resources which were taken over by OPEC. However, if one looks at the profits of the major international oil companies, they digested that with hardly a hiccup. The profits of Exxon, which were about $1,300 million in 1971, have moved steadily upward to over $4 billion by 1979.
If we take the top 31 petroleum companies in Canada for the same period, profits went from $559 million to $3,075 million in 1979.
When Alberta changed its take from 22 per cent to 45 per cent of the dollar, again the industry in Canada was able to adjust to that. The industry has been able to adjust to new conditions and I am sure that will continue.
If the industry considers there is bad news in the budget arrangements, remember that there is also a lot of good news. In the same way Jack Armstrong and Bill Richards have said that they can see opportunities within it, keep in mind that for Canada conversion to gas will mean new markets for gas. Pipelines to be built to the east will mean new markets for western gas. The gas bank will help the smaller companies. There will be greater incentives for Canadian companies and preference for them in future gas exports. All of these things, I suggest, are very helpful signs which are being overlooked by some people in the west at this moment in time.
Any further remarks I have on the matter, I will make on another occasion, but I want to say that the government of Alberta has its priorities and its point of view. But I believe that the government of Alberta is wrong in feeling that it should take so much. It is my hope that understanding and dialogue will reconcile the differences which presently exist between the federal government and the government of Alberta, differences which are harmful to the country we all love.

speechtext:
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Waddell:
That the proclamation laid before the House on Wednesday, November 12, 1980, pursuant to subsection 35(2) of the Petroleum Administration Act, as proclaimed in PC 1980-2915, be revoked.

Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable regret that I rise today to speak on the proclamations issued by the government under the Petroleum Administration Act. Member after member from this side of the House for the past two days has described the tragic implications the government's energy policy will have for the economy, energy security, and federal-provincial relations.
Canada is losing companies which provide necessary jobs, expertise and capital and other spin-offs which enable this country to enjoy its current high standard of living. Right across this country, including the manufacturing and service heartland of Ontario and Quebec, the situation is about to change. Economic and political uncertainty is about to engulf Canada at the very time Canadians are seeking ways and means to become more united and less dependent upon the help of others.
Today I want to shift the focus of the debate a little bit. My colleagues in the Progressive Conservative Party have shown the incompetence of the government's policy. They have shown how Canadian families, families in my constituency, will be paying about $300 more for the cost of energy than they would have had to pay under the Crosbie budget. My colleagues have shown how the security of oil supply has been decreased as a result of these measures. Rather than achieving energy selfsufficiency by 1990, as our government proposed, we hear of threats to close down the Cold Lake project. We hear of cutbacks in exploration programs by Canadian independents. My colleagues have shown how employment will be hurt across the country.
The deferral of the oil sands project in Alberta means that Ontario and Quebec will share almost equally the economic hardships of Liberal policy as private companies cut their

November 25, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act
exploration budgets or move to the United States. Almost daily we hear reports from my part of the country of shutdowns or of lay-offs taking place in industries in Ontario. These industries are affected by the decline in orders from western Canada, which are affected, as well, by the deterioration in the atmosphere and relations in Canada today. Western Canadians are looking for other sources of goods, instead of looking toward central Canada, because of the policies of this government. Yet the government cynically prepares to strike a deal with Saudi Arabia on the grounds, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said, "of security of supply". And we find the government is not serious in its dealings with Alberta, a Canadian province.
As Canadians go jobless, OPEC is receiving the equivalent of $900 a year for each Canadian family. Members of our party have shown that the Canadian oil industry, despite the government's claims to the contrary, is being hit seriously, particularly through the 8 per cent de facto royalty. As Canadian companies move south, the only Canadianizing effect of this energy policy is to create more government ownership. By 1983 this may well range between 45 per cent and 50 per cent, not 24 per cent, as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) would lead us to believe.
I ask the question: will it help national unity? Clearly the answer is no. The invoking of the Petroleum Administration Act will do more than perhaps any other measure taken by the government to damage the country.
Finally, my colleagues have described the impact of the regressive energy policy and the effects that it will have upon consumers and, particularly, on the low-income family. The government has made no provision to allow energy tax credits, like my government's budget did.
1 would point out as well that this government has imposed taxation upon heating oils which affect many poorer families in my constituency who do not have the option of converting to natural gas, and yet we find the government is not apologetic about its policies and is prepared to continue in this vein. This is divisive and punitive for the Canadians who can least afford to pay for it.
There is another aspect of this budget that is largely forgotten. In part, it is a consequence of complacency among members throughout the House, but it is also caused by the fact that the party opposite has ruled this country for so long that it has confused governing with government. Over the year the power of government has increased dramatically. Bureaucracy and public ownership now count for over 40 per cent of our gross national product.
I am not of the belief that government need be inherently bad. On the contrary, I think every member of this House would recognize that government has a vital role to play. However, when the elected representatives in Parliament unnecessarily delegate their task of governing to non-elected bureaucrats, or to a few select cabinet ministers, government becomes a monolithic entity, insensitive to the needs of people, subject to incompetency or, worse, deceit. I am not, therefore, inclined to give powers freely to any body or agency that has
not been elected by the people to govern for the good of this country. Yet, with the invoking of division II of part II of the Petroleum Administration Act, this is precisely what the government has chosen to do.
I am reminded of the warnings that the long time member, friend and former colleague of mine, Hon. Ged Baldwin, gave at the time of the passing of the Petroleum Administration Act in June, 1975. He warned of a government practice that had grown steadily since the end of the Second World War. The delegation of legislative powers to non-elected government agencies or bodies was increasing yearly and becoming more widespread. Civil servants and bureaucrats were making legislative decisions that were directly affecting the lives of every Canadian. But while Mr. Baldwin recognized that delegated legislation is an historically accepted and necessary method of governing, he warned that it was not a method that should be contemplated unless it was clearly necessary and specific in detail as to the extent of the delegation.
In the past Canada has had dangerous experiences with delegated powers which not only threatened the supremacy of Parliament but also the liberty of the people. In December, 1945, for example, Parliament passed a national emergency transitional powers bill which declared that a condition of emergency still existed in Canada, despite the fact that the war had ended. Very substantial powers under the War Measures Act were delegated to the governor in council until this period of emergency was over. In a few months it was discovered that the governor in council had secretly passed an order giving the minister of justice authority to issue an order to interrogate and detain "in such place and under such conditions as he may from time to time determine" any person whom he believed to be likely to communicate information to a foreign agent. This order provided the authority for the arrest, interrogation, and detention of suspects in the great spy investigation of 1946. The arbitrary nature of this piece of legislation, and the degree to which many innocent citizens' rights were revoked, best illustrate how delegated legislation of the variety found in the invoked portion of the Petroleum Administration Act can be abused when Parliament freely chooses to forsake its role of governing. These emergency powers remained in effect until 1954.
This type of abuse of delegated legislation is by no means the exception to the rule. In my capacity as co-chairman of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, I have seen literally dozens of cases where delegated legislation has been abused by both the executive and non-elected agencies. In the case of the former, the committee found, and I quote from the fourth report tabled in the House last July that:
Far too many statutes contain little or no indication of legislative policy and are neutral documents the object of which is merely to confer powers on the executive to act in certain vaguely defined fields. Moreover, these powers are granted in very broad terms so that little or no detail is given as to the content or type of delegated legislation that can be made.

November 25, 1980

In the case of enabling powers, the committee found that it was:
Far too great a temptation to departments and to ministers to grant general enabling powers and to rely on their exercise being confined to the 'four corners of the act.' They are certain, and the committee speaks in the light of its predecessors' experience, to be used, and probably abused, in the pursuit of administrative convenience, to make subordinate laws never imagined by parliamentarians at the time of passage of a bill.
That is what our report had to say on the subject. To combat the further abuse of delegated legislation, the committee recommended that the intention of Parliament in delegating powers and the scope of the legislation be explained beyond all doubt and clearly limited.
Ged Baldwin was the first to recognize that the Petroleum Administration Act was a prime example of the type of faulty legislation the committee was criticizing. Members will remember that during the 1975 debate on the Petroleum Administration Act, the government of the day assured the House that the main intent of the legislation was to provide a base for the export charge which had been used for the purpose of funding the compensation program. The objective was, according to the government, to create a single national price subject only to differences for transportation costs.
Almost as an afterthought, the minister of energy, mines and resources at that time, mentioned that the bill provided a mechanism for the setting of oil and natural gas prices in Canada. Ged Baldwin, on the other hand, pointed out during the debate that articles 36 and 40 to 44 entitled the federal government to fix the price of oil, "despite the fact that a considerable percentage of the crude is not exported." Though Liberal members at that time shouted, "What do these comments have to do about the bill?", 1 think history has justified Mr. Baldwin's concerns, for articles 36 and 40 to 44 are all part of division II of part II. currently being invoked by the Liberal majority in Parliament. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, not enough members heeded his warning in 1975 and in subsequent amending debates on the bill, so we are obligated to take up his crusade today in the hope that parliamentarians on both sides of the House will come to their senses and reject any recourse to the invoking of the Petroleum Administration Act.
Failing this, I would like the government to take a second look at the implication of articles 38 to 47 of the act. The invoking of the Petroleum Administration Act does far more than give the government the power to set prices unilaterally for oil and gas. If this were not bad enough, sections 38 to 47 give the governor in council the power to delegate broad and sweeping licensing provisions to its regulatory agency, the National Energy Board. Section 38 provides that the "governor in council may, by order, direct that the National Energy Board assume supervision and regulation of the movement of crude oil out of an exporting province."
Section 39 further states that where such an order has been received, the movement of all oil out of an exporting province becomes "subject to a licensing system operated by the board". The governor in council then gives the agency a free hand to impose terms and conditions on licences it issues for, first,
Petroleum Administration Act
selling crude oil for consumption outside the exporting province; second, purchasing any crude oil for consumption outside the exporting province; third, acquiring any crude oil for consumption outside the exporting province; and fourth, selling or purchasing outside the exporting province any crude oil from the exporting province.
These licences may be restricted or limited as to area, quantity or time, quality or kind of crude oil. They may be revoked or suspended under section 84 of the National Energy Board Act when the board, after giving a licensee a hearing, forms the opinion that the licensee has violated or failed to comply with the terms or conditions of his licence. In short, the significance of the licensing system is that once it is in place, all selling, transporting, collecting, and mixing of crude oil for purposes elsewhere than in the exporting provinces, would be illegal unless the person engaged in the transaction was a party to the licensing system. Moreover, the act provides a broad range of penalties for breach of prohibitions under section 45(1) and (2).
While the Petroleum Administration Act would appear to provide a great deal of power to at least a few elected representatives via the governor in council, article 46(B) implies that the National Energy Board may be free of whatever restraining influences that the governor in council may have. Section 46(B) reads that the governor in council may make representations, and I quote:
Respecting the duration of licences, the quantities of crude oil that may be sold, purchased or moved under licences and the terms and conditions that may be prescribed by the board in respect of licences.
Unfortunately, the governor in council may choose, either intentionally or unintentionally, not to exercise this option. As I understand it, the word "respecting" in the article could lead the governor in council to subdelegate his law-making authority to the National Energy Board or to the minister.
Members can envisage a regulation by the governor in council which stipulates that the duration of licences or quantities shall be such as the minister notifies the board, or, shall be such as the board shall from time to time determine, and so on. That sort of provision is not uncommon. More important, perhaps, the governor in council may exempt, or empower the minister or the board to exempt, particular individuals from the regulatory requirement as to duration, quantities, or terms and conditions. In short, those sections, 38 to 47, that I have just described, postulate the possibility of a tightly controlled licensing system, containing many potentially arbitrary features governing the movement of oil in and without Canada.
Parliament in the first place should never have passed legislation that so limited its powers over actions by the government concerning the movement of oil in Canada so that the possibility of abuse could arise. I have pointed out how, in the past, broad and sweeping legislation of the variety here before us led to infringement of the principle of the supremacy of Parliament and of individual liberty itself. Today, with respect to the articles I have just described, one could hypothesize numerous examples of how the governor in council, or the National Energy Board, or the minister, or all of them to-

November 25, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act
gether, might well abuse the power Parliament granted the government in 1975.
It is possible, under this act, that the government, in pursuit of its goal of "nationalization" of the oil industry in Canada, might choose to licence only PetroCan for the task of moving oil across Canada. The powers in this act would allow the governor in council, or the National Energy Board, or the minister, to cut short the duration of licences to private companies, Canadian or otherwise. They could determine how much oil was sold or purchased by private licences, and impose arbitrary terms on them.
Moreover, and this is an intent that I cannot believe the current government would harbour, the article in division II of part 11 of the Petroleum Administration Act could even govern the extent to which all or some exports from a producing province could be curtailed or stopped altogether. Shockingly, whether or not the government realizes it now, a future Liberal administration might use the licensing provisions of the Petroleum Administration Act to force Alberta into an energy deal. It could legally threaten Alberta to compromise on price or suffer the consequences of a cut-off from its export market.
It is important to remove even the temptation of this type of abuse from the hands of a select few members of the cabinet, or an individual minister, or a non-elected board.
1 understand the government's policy to establish prices below world levels that has led it to invoke the relevant proclamation of the Petroleum Administration Act. Though I disagree with the policy, if the setting of prices is the only concern of the government, why has it asked that all the licensing provisions in division II of part II be invoked also? A check with the National Energy Board reveals that no orders appear to have been made with respect to regulation by the board under section 38. This is commendable, but not entirely reassuring.
If the government's stated energy goals are to achieve a fair blended price and to achieve a large degree of Canadian ownership, it is vital that the means used to achieve these goals are legitimate and based on the underlying principles of Canada's constitutional order. As such, the means used to achieve the goals of government can be far more important than the ends themselves.
To paraphrase from the standing joint committee's report, it is no exaggeration to say that the evolution of Canada's constitutional system since the Magna Carta has consisted of a series of conflicts over means. Administrative efficiency may be the primary goal of the administrative process, but for the community as a whole the means in this process bear upon an individual's liberties, harmony, and constitutional balance. Since I have heard no public attempt to justify the invoking of articles 38 to 47, balance and fairness in our constitutional and parliamentary system dictate that this section be dropped from the current discussions.
After all, if the government has not even explained why these articles need be invoked, why should Parliament grant these extraordinary licensing powers that delegate these regulations to others and effectively undermine provincial ownership of land, mines and minerals granted under section 109 of the British North America Act? Surely Parliament ought to have a continuing influence over the means by which the government's actions are achieved, and surely the ownership of these lands ought at least to give the provinces some authority to decide to whom their oil will be exported and in what quantity, quality, and time frame. Sections 38 to 47 are over-kill. They are unjustified. They are unnecessary. They are just plain irresponsible, if invoked as the government currently plans to do.
There is more here than meets the eye. I have shown how delegated authority has been abused in the past and described the relevant sections of the Petroleum Administration Act that might be abused in the future. I have cited examples of cases where individual liberties were subverted and the power of Parliament curtailed, and related these to hypothetical situations that could arise if articles 38 to 47 of this act are invoked. I have tried to point out to the government how procedure is the handmaiden of liberty, and the lack of any intent to abuse the powers granted to the governor in council, the minister or the National Energy Board, is no excuse for their failure to drop articles 38 to 47 from the proclamation of the Petroleum Administration Act.
Finally, I have tried to show members of both sides of the House that it is the duty of this Parliament to say no to the minister's proclamation of an act that gives a select few, elected and non-elected members of government, blanket authority over petroleum pricing and licensing in this country. It is about time that Parliament began reasserting its independence and supremacy over delegated legislation that can be potentially dangerous to the underlying constitutional principles and individual liberties of the country.
Member after member who has spoken in this debate so far has dealt with the question of the effect of the government's policies on the unity of Canada and upon energy security in Canada. The minister responsible for fitness and amateur sport, who spoke a few minutes ago, dealt with what he felt was an urgent need to protect the rights of consumers in Canada. I do not think there is a member in this House or any Canadian who is not concerned about the effect of higher energy prices upon average Canadians, but I think it is essential to remind the government that the arbitrary power it is asking for today-and we ask for justification-is having a serious effect on the national fabric of Canada itself.
We hear it said from time to time in Ottawa and throughout the country that Ontarians should be happy with what the government is doing in that Ontarians benefit, conceivably, in the short term from this federal intervention in an area which falls under provincial jurisdiction, and that to the extent to which Ottawa is able to expropriate energy wealth from the producing provinces it is to the benefit of consumers.
The hon. member from the NDP who spoke earlier pointed out that it was not the Albertans who ran up the $14.5 billion
November 25, 1980

deficit which the federal government faces today but that it is the Albertans who find their wealth confiscated by this government to pay for that deficit. My friend from the NDP did not say where he was when there were discussions in this House about high federal deficits and that this money will be used to finance them.
We were here.

They were here, they were active, and they voted in every single instance to increase spending in Canada and not to decrease it. Nonetheless, I am glad to see this afternoon at least a late-blooming appreciation of the fact that what is happening here is the expropriation of the wealth of one portion of the country to pay for the federal government's inability to control its own spending.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, some people will argue that Ontarians will benefit from that and that we should be happy to see this happens. If they believe that this is so, they seriously misread the mood of my home province. Since confederation it has been Ontario which has been a central force for the unity of this country, and it has argued in all instances that all portions of this country have to be dealt with fairly and equitably. Confederation cannot simply be there as the thumb upon the scales to benefit one region of the country to the disfavour of others.
Ontarians today are deeply concerned when they see the effects of the policies of this government, which damage the unity of this country and make it difficult for us to live our lives in a feeling of harmony, of common sense and of good will, which is so essential if we are to overcome the centrifugal forces in our country which threaten to tear it apart. Ontarians are not happy to see what the federal government is doing. They are deeply concerned about their country and they deeply oppose any actions taken by this government which pit Canadian against Canadian, and which make more difficult our job of fostering a sense of national unity.
As a member of Parliament from a small town and rural area with many constituents who are not wealthy, I am deeply concerned about the effects of this government's policies. When ministers say these policies are necessary to hold prices down, I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that the effect of the government's energy policies is to drive prices up. It was this government that imposed a tax upon the heating oil which is used by large numbers of my constituents who do not have recourse to natural gas. Yet these are the people who are being hit by the policies of this government, ostensibly brought down to give protection to the consumers and to protect the national interest. It is my constituents who are being deprived of an energy tax credit which was proposed in the Crosbie budget.
Where is the government when it talks about concern for consumers in this country and when it talks about the problems of individual Canadian families? Where are ministers when those families ask for assistance from the government in the form of an energy tax credit which was promised by the former government to help compensate for higher prices? Where is this government when constituents in my constituen-
Petroleum Administration Act
cy and in constituencies like mine across Ontario find their jobs being taken away from them because of slowdowns in the economy as a result of this government's policies?
I do not think my constituents will be fooled into believing that slowdowns in oil exploration and development in western Canada will not have a very serious effect upon their jobs right here in the heartland of Canada, because it is Ontario which benefits most from the manufacturing which is required to supply the oil industry, and a slowdown in that industry affects jobs right here in the industrial heartland of Canada.
This government campaigned against the energy policy proposed by our government, which would have encouraged exploration and development in Canada and which would have given massive assistance to the search for alternative sources of energy, much of that development money going into Ontario. I ask hon. members opposite how they can justify policies which today are costing the jobs of Ontarians.
There is a sense of malaise and uncertainty-which I have not felt before in my constituency over the course of the past eight years-which I feel today when I go around it. Canadians are frightened not just about whether their children will have jobs but also about whether they will be able to hang on to their own jobs because the effect of this government's policies is to take those jobs away. Hon. members opposite would happily pay the Saudi Arabians twice what they would pay Canadians to supply oil for Canadian needs. They would happily see that money leave Canada entirely, as well as industrial benefits going elsewhere instead of staying in Canada where they would provide jobs for Canadians. They would happily see the effects of their policies, which will be to drive exploration and development out of Canada and take jobs from Canada into the United States where development of the oil industry is very welcome.
This is not an issue on which the government can expect to divide Alberta from the rest of Canadians. All of Canada suffers from the consequences of the incompetence on energy issues of this government. All of Canada had a right to expect, after the last election, that the government would keep its promises and bring in measures which would actually stimulate Canadian ownership and do something to encourage employment in Canada, yet what we have found is that promise after promise has been broken. If Canadians liked what was done to them by the Prime Minister with respect to wage and price controls, they will love what he is doing to them with respect to the energy promises and employment promises which he made during the 1980 election.
What the government is doing today is inflicting serious damage upon the unity of Canada and affecting very grievously the jobs of Canadians. I do not believe that a member on any side of the House, whether in the opposition or in the government, has any right to stand here and support such a measure, and I call upon hon. members on all sides of the House to join with the members of my party in saying to the government that these measures may not go forward and that

November 25, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act
the time has come not to sit down with Saudi sheiks, but to sit down with the people of Alberta, who are Canadians, first, and to work out a regime of pricing and development which is fair to all Canadians and which would put Canadian interests first. That is all Canadians are asking for, and I think they are entitled to no less.
