speechtext:
Before proposing the question on Bill C-206 to amend the Canada Labour Code, the Chair ought to register reservations and enter a caveat as to the procedural acceptability of the bill. The Chair is of the view that certain provisions of the bill may involve expenditures of public funds, which can only be authorized by way of a royal recommendation. However, since the Chair does not want to take too much time of private members' hour to rule now, I intend to allow the debate on the bill, without prejudice to the decision which may have to be made on the procedural acceptability of the bill at the conclusion of the debate at second reading.
November 25, 1980

For immediate reference I would refer to clauses 2 and 3 in which there is a suggestion, if I understand the bill correctly, that there may be a requirement for the expenditure of government funds in so far as Crown corporations are concerned. That is the essence of the caveat being entered by the Chair. The hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) may choose to raise that point during his own remarks on the bill, but for the moment it seems to be the best way to proceed.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND WITH RESPECT TO MATERNITY LEAVE
speechtext:
that Bill C-206, to amend the Canada Labour Code (maternity leave), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have noted your caveat on the admissibility of my bill in terms of the expenditure of public funds through Crown corporations. When the Chair is considering the matter, I should like it to take into consideration that I do not believe the caveat applies, because in effect my bill calls for leave without pay. I do not know how Crown corporations, any other business, or all employees under federal jurisdiction, would call for extra expenditures.
Bill C-206 has been on the order paper for some time. It would increase the maximum period of maternity leave which is presently in the Canada Labour Code from 17 weeks to 52 weeks. It would provide up to three years of maternity leave for the employee whose child requires constant care. It would allow an employee to credit maternity leave time toward pension plans or any benefits determined by seniority. That means if an employee chooses, when on leave without pay or after coming back to work, to make payments toward her pension plan or contributions to the Canada Pension Plan, then the employer would match the contributions, which I think does not come under the caveat Mr. Speaker mentioned earlier. The final provision of the bill would be that if an employee were to die during childbirth, or after the child is born, the spouse would be entitled to the remaining leave and benefits.
If the bill were to pass, two other things must happen. It applies only to industries and employers under federal jurisdiction; the provinces would have to be encouraged to pass similar legislation. The federal government should amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to increase the length of maternity benefits which at present is only 15 weeks. This change was not included in my private member's bill because of the risk that the entire bill might be ruled out of order in that it would involve the spending of money. I tried to keep in mind the business about a private member's bill calling for the expenditure of money. Where unemployment insurance benefits are involved, it would be up to the government to bring in its amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act to coincide with the provisions of my bill.
There are a lot of reasons why this legislation is long over due. The importance of bonding in the first year of a child's life cannot be overemphasized. Close ties between parent and child affect the child's behaviour for the rest of its life. This has been verified by experts in the field, and it was pointed out as recently as last October in the Senate subcommittee report
Canada Labour Code
entitled "Child at Risk". I invite hon. members to read what the committee reported about good parenting being of overwhelming importance to the developing personality of a child. Extended maternity leave is one of the important means of achieving those close ties.
Maternity leave is no longer a fringe benefit for a selected few who can negotiate it through collective agreements. Women have been entering the labour force in increasing numbers, and can no longer be dismissed as a secondary labour force. In 1979, 49 per cent of the women in Canada, or almost half, were in the paid work force. Between 1969 and 1979 the growth of women in the work force increased by over 61 per cent. The main child-bearing years are between the years of 20 and 44. Last year 63 per cent of working women in Canada were between those ages. There has been concern about Canada's declining birth rate. The 52 weeks of maternity leave could offer further job security to women who want to have children but are reluctant to risk their job security, their pay level, their economic and social well-being.
There have been too many instances across the country where an employee has requested time off from work to bear a child and to spend some time with the child after birth, and after two or three months has been told by her employer, "Well, you have had so much time off; if you cannot get back to work within the next month or two, I will have to hire someone else."
This is not a new provision in other parts of the world. I am asking that Canada catch up with a lot of other places. Also I remind the House that under the Financial Administration Act and the Public Service Staff Relations Act federal public servants are allowed 37 weeks of maternity leave-up to 11 weeks before birth and 26 weeks after. It is an improvement over what is in the Canada Labour Code. So surely the government cannot object to improving the Canada Labour Code, compared to the provisions affecting federal public servants. I should like to mention what is occurring in other countries. Austria, Norway and the Soviet Union provide one-year leave for maternity; Czechoslovakia provides two years; Spain and Bulgaria provide three years. I find it somewhat embarrassing that we are behind these other countries.
There is another reason why I think this matter is important. Just the other day another private member's bill was before the House concerning abortion. All of us in the chamber have been required to go through the agonizing and heart-rending feelings of hon. members on both sides of the question, feelings that are sincerely held and believed in. I think this provision, as well as a number of others, would do more to end the perceived need and demand for abortion. It is one of many measures which I think would reduce a need for abortion that is not only perceived but which also may be real.
It seems to me that people do not resort to abortion because they suddenly do not love babies. It is because they find themselves caught in a frightening and terrifying squeeze where there is no housing, no job, no health, no acceptance or

November 25, 1980
Canada Labour Code
support. I think all hon. members want to do all they can to restructure our society and make it a hospitable place in which to live. We want to reduce substantially the perceived and felt need for abortion. Of equal importance is the necessity for a mother to be with her new baby, and a one year leave of absence without pay would help. Unless she belongs to a union, if she is lucky enough to have one, she can through a collective agreement negotiate some additional benefits. That is fine. Surely the federal law should set out a minimum of 12 months leave from the position that woman held with her employer, and guarantee her right to return to it, or to a better position with the same employer. This is only one of many things we need to do to strengthen the parent or mother-child bonding, to strengthen families and reduce their perceived compulsion or need for abortion, and to make this a more decent, understanding society than it presently is.
I am aware the government is looking at amendments to the Canada Labour Code. I do not care if it is my bill that passes, or a bill put forward by an opposition member, or a government bill, as long as it gets done. Would the minister or his parliamentary secretary at least agree when they bring in amendments to the Canada Labour Code that the subject matter of this bill be referred to the standing committee so that the government can decide whether or not to incorporate the provisions of my bill into their legislation? I will be among the first to applaud and congratulate them for it. This is not the kind of issue for prima donnas or any one person to take credit for. Members from all parties have advocated this and have spoken in favour of it for many years.
1 find it difficult to understand why it takes so long to resolve an issue about which there can easily be all party agreement, which can do much to reduce the divisions that occur among members of Parliament, as well as among Canadians, on social and moral issues, abortion being one of them. It seems to me the way to solve divisions is to bring in a number of measures.
It is not sufficient just to guarantee employment and leaves of absence for women to bear children. There is a host of other wide-sweeping reforms needed to strengthen families, to strengthen the love, care and the ability to care for children. A measure of economic security for single parent families must be enhanced. There must be more daycare centres in a massive way, not just through provincial, municipal and federal governments, but employers must and should make significant contributions to women at work for their children to be cared for while at work. So many of them must work because they want a house and to raise and love a family.
Mr. Speaker, chartered banks must be required to set aside a portion of their investment capital into the area of low-interest mortgages-like 8 per cent. This must be done so that mortgage rates will no longer cripple young families or, even worse, prevent them from having decent housing.
Medicare must be universal. It is something all of us are proud of. I will not just brag about Saskatchewan. It must be the norm throughout society so that it, too, can aid in the well-being of mothers and their newborn.
1 submit federal funding must be made available to provinces and educational institutions to enable them to provide all forms of birth control and family planning information, not just for students but for parents. This would encourage responsibility and decrease the ignorance which exists on those subjects. It would enable each individual, and more particularly women, to be informed intelligently and it would enable them to adopt a method of birth control which best meets their own religious beliefs, economic, social and family needs. It is a decision they should be able to make in an informed and intelligent manner.
Mr. Speaker, this bill of mine is only one of many steps which must be taken in order to improve our society. I end my speech by quoting a statement released by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops. It has proven of great value to me. It reads:
To be involved in the task of making this society hospitable to life, is a foremost requirement of social justice. That is why we must take most seriously the rebuke that those who oppose abortion care too little about the special problems of mothers and the burdens of rearing children once they are born. If respect for life seems to end with birth, our perceptions and values are truncated and incomplete. The call of Christ, that we should bear one another's burdens, demands that we reach out in practical ways to share all the burdens of parenthood. The indicated aid and support will include working to change economic and social realities in the direction of justice and respect for life. From doing this, we must not flinch.
Mr. Speaker, whatever one's religious beliefs are, or if one has no religious beliefs, that is a statement that all of us can agree with and support. My bill, in its own limited way, calls for the implementing of one of many measures that needs to be taken to make this a more decent society, one that is more hospitable in which to live for mothers and families in our country.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND WITH RESPECT TO MATERNITY LEAVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few important remarks on Bill C-206 now before the House.
First of all, I should like to express my unmitigated admiration for the architect of the bill, the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), who obviously acted under the inspiration of altruistic principles. The hon. member shows an awareness of and an interest in the well-being of Canadian women at work, well-being which often is not protected enough.
Hon. members are probably all aware that in almost all parts of the country federal and provincial statutes apply which give some form of protection to women at work, particularly with regard to maternity leave. To those must be added two international instruments that deal with maternity benefits, namely, the United Nations Declaration of 1967 on the elimination of discrimination against women which stipulates that "In order to prevent discrimination against women by reason of marriage or maternity and to guarantee their effective right to work, steps must be taken to keep them from being fired when they marry or bear children, and to provide for maternity leave with pay and the guarantee of returning to
November 25, 1980

their former job, as well as to ensure that they benefit from required social services, including child care."
Convention 103 of the International Labour Organization on maternity protection, the second international instrument, was never ratified by Canada because it considered it obsolete in several regards. In fact, the ILO itself is in the process of reviewing and reinforcing the provisions now applicable so as to bring them more into line with the current needs of all workers who are breadwinners. Here in Canada, the Labour Code, the basic federal statute in the matter, is also being revised.
The Women's Bureau has played a major role in this regard and the department has used much of its resources to promote work equality. Mr. Speaker, the principle of work equality includes several important components, and the hon. members will undoubtedly be interested to learn which factors are considered essential to define equitable treatment. In the simplest possible terms, the first factor concerns reasonable access to leave for the worker in charge of a family. The second concerns the elimination of inherent obstacles to hiring which prevent women from getting the better paid jobs and from developing fully on a professional level. The third is related to a job-evaluation method which would simplify application of the equal pay for equal work concept. The fourth concerns the elimination of any harassment in the workplace and of any behaviour which perpetuates discrimination and constitutes a threat to the job and performance of women workers. Finally, the setting up of an administrative structure to monitor, if need be, and apply the work equality concept would ensure true equality in the work place.
I have referred to prejudice and discrimination which are unfortunately still present in various aspects of the work place. Work segregation, unequal pay for men and women and sexual intimidation are a few of the practices which create and maintain a climate of inequality in the workplace. Many other factors can also come into play, such as the negative effects on a career of absence from work because of the adoption or the birth of a child. Then, there is the leave forced upon the workers concerned. The list is long and there are still many prejudices. One of the most difficult issues to define in this regard is the responsibility of private businesses in relation to that of the parents.
In that respect, as was previously mentioned, the government recently did an over-all survey of the situation here in Canada and in some other countries, and carefully considered and assessed the rules that apply in the industry, all legal provisions, as well as the latest trends. That survey has now been completed, I believe. Very shortly the government plans to introduce into the Canadian Labour Code a package of amendments based on this survey. I think we will thus be in a position to satisfy the more pressing needs. I am sure that Canada will show leadership in providing equal work opportunity.
Canada Labour Code
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer hon. members to a recent book published by James Bennett and Pierre Loewe entitled "Women in Business". Its subtitle is: "A shameful waste of human resources." The book shows that in the vast majority of businesses in Canada not only are women treated as second-class citizens but they are also victims of both conscious and unconscious discrimination. I for one can only applaud the fact that at the federal level at least forthcoming serious legislative amendments will be fighting this type of discrimination so that all workers having family responsibilities may work in a more equitable environment.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND WITH RESPECT TO MATERNITY LEAVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this carefully-thought-out bill which would be a real addition to the social legislation of this country. Even though a caveat has been placed on the bill, I urge the government side to let it proceed through second reading so that it may be fully discussed in committee.
I am astounded by the number of excellent bills that are talked out in this House during second reading when only the principle of a bill, not the clause by clause detail, is being discussed. The reasons these bills are talked out are not very apparent. A bill should be defeated only after very careful consideration in committee. This particular bill should not be talked out, for many reasons.
Many of the points raised by the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), who introduced the bill, are points which can be supported by almost every political party, religious organization, or facet of our society. Since I began my career in federal politics I have always been bothered by the red tape expectant working mothers must go through to obtain unemployment insurance benefits. I am sure all hon. members are acquainted with studies which indicate that the period before the birth of a child is very important to the health and stability of the child. If the mother is worried or ill at ease about what will happen after the birth of the child, it is bound to have an adverse affect on its health and well-being when it is born.
The hon. member who introduced the motion indicated that 52 weeks maternity leave would reduce the incidence of abortion, and I believe he is correct. No matter whether one is in favour of or opposed to abortion, one must be concerned with the increase in the number of abortions in the country, a number which increases every year. While I was a member of the Alberta legislature I asked for a report which would indicate how many women had gone through the medicare program to obtain an abortion more than once. I was astounded to hear that some women had experienced three or four abortions. The first time may have been a mistake or a concern, but some women have experienced three or four abortions. Abortion is being used as a birth control method with which I completely disagree.

November 25, 1980
Canada Labour Code
When one looks at all of the factors leading to abortion, in my view the economic one is the one that comes up most often. The girl or woman is concerned about how she will keep the wolf from the door or about how she will make a living. I attended a type of profile meeting a week ago. I believe everyone there was opposed to abortion. But a woman came up and spoke to me. She said quietly that she had experienced an abortion herself when she was in her late teens. She told me that the anguish she suffered still awakened her at night when she thought about aborting her child who would now be 19 or 20 years of age. She told me that her prime reason for aborting the child was the lack of livelihood and she could not see how she could keep the child. These reasons were the ones which led her to have an abortion. I believe the economic factor is a very important one in a great number of cases where abortion is carried out. It is not the factor in everyone, but certainly it is in a large number. 1 do not know exactly what the percentage is, but I would say that about one-third of the abortions are due to economic reasons.
If that is so, this bill, if it reduces the number of abortions by one-third in this country, would be a wonderful thing. Who knows what wonderful children might be born. These children would grow into adults. We do not know what they can do for the world or the genius that we might be killing because of these abortions.
The 52-week maternity leave would be a major factor in changing the mind, or at least eliminating the worry of a girl, who otherwise might agree to an abortion.
We all talk about making the workplace a place where women and men are equal. In many cases, this is not so. In many cases it is impossible to make them equal. In my view, men and women will never be close to being equal unless we recognize that women bear children. If women are going to be penalized when they have a child, either through a reduction in benefits or through a reduction in chances for promotion, then equality goes straight out of the window. This situation happens many times. At a teachers' meeting I heard someone say that Mrs. so and so could qualify as the vice principal if she were not married. They were afraid she might have a child and be absent. Absence in those days was not very much, I can tell you. As a matter of fact, it was embarrassing for those who were pregnant and had to work up to within a month or perhaps even a couple of weeks of giving birth. It was embarrassing to them and embarrassing to all of their loved ones. If we are going to have equality in the work place between men and women we have to recognize that childbirth is something a woman naturally wants. If she does have a child then the woman should not be penalized because of it. Otherwise, we are simply talking about equality with our lips and forgetting all about it as far as our hearts and minds are concerned.
The federal government can be commended for giving 11 weeks maternity leave prior to birth. That is almost three months. The last three months is an embarrassing period of time. This is a time when a woman should not be bothered with the frustrations of the everyday workplace. However, I
would like to see that time extended to three months at least and possibly more in some cases depending on doctors' advice. But 11 weeks is certainly far in advance of what many employers are giving today to women who are bearing children.
If the 52-week period were granted, it would bring a sense of stability to married women who want to raise a family. Women should not be denied the contribution they will make through raising a family and looking after a family simply because there may be some inconvenience in the workplace. Inconvenience has to be put down as an item which will lead to a better country and a better community. If the number of children born is reduced through artificial methods or economic factors, then the future of the country is really at stake.
I think a pope said once that the first seven years of a child's life were the most important years. It has been said that if people could have the care of a child for the first seven years they would not worry about what happened after that. The foundation of what that child will do has been established in the first seven years of life. Researchers have indicated that the period before birth is also a vitally important time in the life of a child. This aspect was dealt with quite excellently by the mover of this bill. The welfare of the child should be the predominating thought in our minds as should be the welfare of the mother. Both of these are considered in this bill where the 52 weeks maximum is permitted for a maternity case.
To get more equality in the workplace, we should eliminate some of the discrimination we see today. Women should not be subject to embarrassment because of pregnancy. The number of abortions in this country should be reduced. We should provide for the healthy future of the child and the mother. I think this bill should be supported and I urge hon. members to give it their full support on second reading.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND WITH RESPECT TO MATERNITY LEAVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that my colleague for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) will allow at least one woman to address this issue. I am not denying him the rights of a father, but I hope that he will at least recognize that I have some rights as a mother.
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to speak of the essence of the matter, of the principle involved, and note that this bill favours parental bonding, and in this regard, I would like to quote for my colleagues one of the statements made in the Senate report entitled "Child at Risk," which was published recently and which is an excellent report, concerning the importance of parental bonding. This report refers to the mother at the time of birth and right after, but I believe that the statement concerning the weeks immediately following birth could also apply to the father. The report says:
November 25, 1980

Today, women are having terrible difficulties in parenting and in knowing how to parent... Therefore, we need those moments that nature gives us, in a sense, to become attached to our infants, to become better mothers, to become more sensitive in relation to infants. It does not mean it won't happen on day three, or two weeks hence;-
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that existing benefits granted through unemployment insurance may not always allow this parental attachment to form or to favour the development of the infant. This is why I must say that I agree with the spirit of Bill C-206 introduced by my colleague from Regina West, which promotes attachment on the part of one of the parents, either the father or the mother, but the emphasis is placed on maternity leave, and in this regard, I must say that the bill may show a certain weakness because I think that it should also apply to the father.
I must say that, as a former administrator of a school board in Quebec, I have had the occasion to apply such a policy of 52 weeks renewable for another year at the request of the teacher. In other words, this policy is already implemented in certain public bodies in the province of Quebec. This is now the policy of the Quebec government, but when we took this initiative, we were able to grant teachers leave so that they might see to the education of their own children, and 1 believe that a country and a government which allow parents to take care of their own children while guaranteeing their jobs are basically taking their responsibilities seriously. Elowever, I must say that I also agree with the clause which guarantees that the employee may continue to contribute toward his fringe benefits. We all know that the federal government is now reviewing the question of pensions, and I believe that such a provision for workers who leave the labour force to have or bring up children is very positive and would solve some of the problems that now exist concerning pensions, especially for women.
As concerns the three years of constant care for children with special problems, I must say that this legislation seems extremely positive to me. I would like to quote in this regard section 80 of the report of the Senate committee concerning emotional privation;
80. The importance of establishing good, affectionate, early attachments has already been mentioned. If this does not happen, the child has lost an opportunity for the optimal early development of a healthy personality-Normally, this person is the mother-In some cases neither parent is able to fulfil the needed role of a steadfast and affectionate presence in the child's life. Such circumstances have been referred to as "parental deprivation". This is "recognized as a prime cause of delinquency and other personality disorders".
This means that in the case of children who might have special problems, it is even more important to grant leave to the parent while protecting his or her job. Obviously, what remains is to set specific criteria to define the situation and grant such leave for a period which could be extended.
1 must say, however, that such a provision cannot be implemented alone without other important measures, namely, an
Canada Labour Code
extended program of daycare centres. As a matter of fact, in its report, the Senate committee mentions the case of a child who can secure a love relationship with another person and of the mother who might not be able to afford 52 weeks leave without pay. A child who can have a love relationship with another person can develop in the normal way after the first few weeks. Therefore, I think that this provision to extend the length of maternity leave and to protect the employment of Canadian male and female workers who have a new child is extremely positive.
However, I think that there is a second shortcoming in the legislation. There is no mention of maternity leave in the context of adoption. I think that, in the case of adoption, maternity leave is equally important and that it enables parents to establish that love relationship with the young child they are going to adopt. I should have liked the bill to be more precise in that regard and to allow that alternative to leave because as a champion of equality for women, I think that if, at a certain time, it were possible for the father to look after the child at home, that proposed leave could be equally shared by the father and the mother. In fact, the report of the Senate committee emphasizes the fact that it is very important for the child, even for a young child, to establish that love relationship with the parents in order to develop harmoniously.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to insist that such a measure should be introduced in the context of a global family policy. We often have pieces of legislation which tend to remedy a problem but which finally do not solve the specific problems a Canadian family can have.

For that reason, I wish the bill could be amended by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan), who is responsible for amendments to the Canada Labour Code, so that this measure could be easily accessible to those with a new baby. I would like to see the measure discussed with the Department of National Health and Welfare in order to provide better child care service for those women who do not have enough revenue to stay home after the birth and receive only unemployment insurance benefits. These women should enjoy decent services. This would help avoid the problem of children in their early stages not receiving proper consideration.
I hope the hon. member for Regina West will take into account that we gladly support this measure, but we feel there are a few items missing. 1 hope the minister will take this as a recommendation and implement it as soon as possible.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Sports)
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND WITH RESPECT TO MATERNITY LEAVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address some pertinent remarks to Bill C-206, an act to amend the Canada Labour Code. The principle intent of this bill is to extend the maximum period of maternity leave to 52 weeks from the present 17. Other amendments would provide for up to three years maternity leave in the case of a child requiring constant care, permit maternity leave to be credited toward a pension

November 25, 1980
Canada Labour Code
plan and, in the case of a mother's death during or after childbirth, transfer to her spouse her remaining leave and other benefits. These, in short, are the main proposals of Bill C-206.
The hon. member's bill strikes a responsive chord, coming as it does on the heels of the settlement of the translators' strike. It would certainly be a wonderful world if the provisions of the kind outlined, such as 52 weeks maternity leave, were generally available. Most legislative provisions across the country today range between 17 and 18 weeks. At the outset, however, 1 think it would be useful if I were to briefly describe existing maternity leave legislation.
As hon. members will be aware, such legislation appears in virtually all Canadian jurisdictions in various forms. The jurisdiction affected by the proposed bill is, of course, the federal jurisdiction.

The federal legislation maternity leave to be found in part III of the Canada Labour Code was passed in 1971. At that time only British Columbia and Ontario had similar legislation. This legislation provided for 17 weeks leave for employees with 12 consecutive months of service with the same employer. The beneficiary could avail herself of this leave 11 weeks before the expected date of delivery and for a period of six weeks following the birth of the child. The legislation ensured security of employment by providing that the employee had the right to get her job back or any similar position without reduction of wages or loss of benefits. Furthermore, upon her return, employment was deemed to have been continuous with regard to the position she held before leave was granted.
In 1975 the legislation on maternity leave became more flexible thanks to Bill C-16. A pregnant employee then became entitled to up to 11 weeks leave prior to the anticipated date of delivery and to up to 17 weeks after the birth of the child. She could also benefit from additional leaves equal to the difference between the estimated and actual dates of delivery. The leave could therefore cover a period of 26 weeks instead of 17 as was the case before. Three years later. Bill C-8 again amended the legislation by improving the security of employment clause which provides that an employer cannot dismiss or lay off an employee on the sole ground that she is pregnant or has asked for leave.

As hon. members may recall, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) earlier this month indicated the board's willingness to offer all federal employees new maternity and paternity benefits. These include the maternity benefits already mentioned, unpaid paternity and adoption leave of up to 26 weeks, some provision for the care of sick family members and medical and adoption appointments.
Following the federal lead, similar legislation now exists in all other jurisdictions in Canada with the exception of Prince
Edward Island, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. The qualification is 12 months continuous service in five jurisdictions, 12 months and 11 weeks in one jurisdiction and 20 weeks in one jurisdiction. Two jurisdictions have no qualification period. The length of the leave period is 16 weeks in one jurisdiction, 17 weeks in five jurisdictions and 18 weeks in three jurisdictions. Only four jurisdictions provide for protection from lay-off or dismissal and, with the exception of two provinces, it is specifically stated that the woman must be reinstated in the same or a similar position. So we can see that the 17-week period is the most commonly applied across Canada.
Beyond these minor differences in legislation there are some jurisdictions which have made some innovative changes to provide the pregnant woman with more job security. For example, in two jurisdictions-Ontario and Saskatchewan- specific mention is made of pregnancy-related illnesses. The legislation in these provinces prohibits employers from discriminating in the provision of sick leave and disability benefits on the basis that the illness is pregnancy-related. The Quebec legislation provides a safety clause which permits the woman who provides a medical certificate to ask for a change of duties if the working conditions are hazardous to her or to the fetus. Also, if the employer does not provide her with alternative employment within eight days, the woman may go on special paid leave up until the commencement of her maternity leave, that is, eight weeks preceding the expected birth.
Provisions for maternity leave also exist in a number of collective agreements in Canada. In 1979 various jurisdictions were surveyed to determine the frequency of maternity leave clauses, and it was found that provisions in existence in various jurisdictions ranged from 10 per cent to 58 per cent of the agreements studied. In general, the clauses followed the provisions of the legislation with some providing for additional leave of up to one year, shorter qualification periods, several weeks of paid leave and continuation of benefits during leave with accumulation of seniority.
However, the majority of union contracts do not provide for any form of maternity leave, relying totally on legislation to provide protection. It must also be noted that of more than four million women in the labour force little more than a quarter are unionized.

In November, 1979, the government of Quebec offered its public and related employees the most interesting provisions regarding parental leave. All agreements are not yet in effect at the present time, but here are some of the clauses they contain: 20 weeks of leave with pay divided as follows: 93 per cent of the salary will be paid to the employee during the two-week waiting period before payment of unemployment benefits; moreover, during the 15-week benefit period, the employer agrees to pay the difference between the amount of the benefits and 93 per cent of the salary and to pay the same portion of the salary during the additional three weeks.
November 25, 1980

Another provision allows extension of maternity leave without pay for a two-year period. This leave is available to the mother or the father. It can also be split between the two. The employee on leave gets credit for seniority, other leave and benefits.
Countries other than Canada have similar legislation and some have made outstanding progress in that respect. Sweden, for example, extends up to two years of leave with pay to either parent. That country also favours part-time work and flexible working hours for parents with children under six. In Sweden, maternity provisions go far beyond leave for confinement and the subsequent recovery period. In that country the legislation provides that parents may take whatever time they need to look after their children. In other words, Sweden has recognized that women are a vital and permanent part of the labour force, and that they can go on with their careers after their children are born.
Such changes did not come about only due to the pressure of the women's liberation movement. They are also derived from economic factors. This means that working conditions have had to adapt themselves to the changes in the role of man and woman in order to promote a healthier family life. The Swedish legislation is quite wide in its scope, and the philosophy underlying it might very well serve as an example here.

South of the border, an increasing number of employers in the United States private sector are taking the lead in introducing creative employment benefits. The latest move in this direction relates to adoption. A recent study of benefit programs offered by 14 large corporations indicates that adoption benefits were established as an equity consideration. The survey found that the infrequency of adoption made the program inexpensive when compared with other benefits, particularly the amount of positive public relations value generated.

speechtext: When the debate was interrupted at five o'clock this afternoon, the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Gingras) had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, when the House took recess at 5 p.m., I was speaking generally of my riding of Abitibi, which is according to the privilege granted to new members in their first session. I referred to its immense

November 25, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act
territory, 750,000 square kilometres, that is 48 per cent of the province of Quebec. I dealt with its contrasts, its history and its rural vocation. At five o'clock, I was broaching the subject of tourism in that part of our country.
The Abitibi region, Mr. Speaker, is a marvellous region for those who love nature; it embraces thousands of lakes and rivers, wide open spaces, and plenty of fresh unpolluted air. It is a small paradise for fishermen and hunters. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind you, if 1 may, that the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) while a young student in the forties canoed down the Harricanaw River to James Bay. No wonder, Mr. Speaker, that he insists on being in good physical shape while he is at the helm of this country of ours.
The Harricanaw River runs within my riding, Mr. Speaker, and flows into James Bay, site of the project of the century. I would like to give a few energy data on the James Bay project. By 1990, the La Grande complex will generate 11,400 megawatts. With the expected excess water, dams could be overequipped to produce 4,652 megawatts more. The NBR project proposed in the same James Bay area will include the Notta-way Broadback and Rupert rivers, with a possible production of 2,870 megawatts. When completed, the whole James Bay program will have a total production of 27,632 megawatts.
I would like to take this opportunity tonight to point out how far-sighted Mr. Robert Bourassa was in giving the go ahead to the project when he was the premier of Quebec.
1 could not make a complete survey of my riding without mentioning forestry. From the small sawmill of the thirties to what we see today, things have changed quite a bit.
We now have modern plants with an increasing capacity to finish products right here. A kraft pulp and paper mill was established at Lebel-sur-Quevillon, a brand new town in existence since 1965. At Val d'Or, we have a particle board plant, and a newspaper mill is now being built at Amos, at a cost of over $190 million, thanks to the regional development assistance granted by DREE. This is the very first newsprint plant to be built in Quebec since 1938. Moreover, it is the only one wholly owned and controlled by Francophones. The plant will use nothing but locally produced energy, that is coming from the riding of Abitibi, electricity coming from James Bay and forest waste products.
That brings me, Mr. Speaker, to the national energy program, and more specifically renewable energy and energy conservation. With regard to the national energy program, allow me to make a few comments concerning sources of renewable energy and the role the government intends to play across the whole spectrum of those energies.
I want to speak today about forests. I quote from page 67 of the document entitled "The National Energy Program":
The federal government currently administers the FIRE (Forest Industries Renewable Energy) program, which provides a substantial grant for forest
industries that convert to wood waste. To encourage even greater displacement of petroleum by biomass fuels, this program will be expanded to apply to other organic materials such as agricultural and municipal wastes, and to cover all industrial and commercial establishments, in all areas. Grants will also be made available to firms that undertake cogeneration of electricity (the generation of electricity and process heat at the plant site). To provide additional flexibility, and make this program attractive even to the largest industries, the existing $4 million upper limit on grants will be removed.
Mr. Speaker, I have here another document entitled ktThe Green Gold." It is an article written by Mr. Louis-Jean Lussier and published in Foret Conservation, August-Septem-ber 1980. I quote:
In this world going through an energy crisis .. . could it be possible that the huge Quebec forests, an essentially renewable resource, replace someday the exhaustible oil of the Arab sheiks, the price of which is skyrocketing every year, somewhat as the whim takes them? From time to time, a daily newspaper looking for a good story will tell you about methanol, this precious fluid made from wood which will soon fire your car engine. And don't you dismiss it as a dream: already in Brazil they use as a motor fuel a mixture of gasoline and 30 per cent methanol known as gasohol.
I will limit my remarks tonight to a concept that is more elementary than gasohol, but which still interests me a great deal. 1 would like to give as an example a public building located in my riding and that building, as everything else in Abitibi, is close to a wood waste burner. In that particular case, the building is close to five such burners.
So, that building uses 250,000 gallons of heating oil or the equivalent of 6,250 barrels of oil. As hon. members know, an imported barrel of oil today costs Canadian taxpayers $21.50 in subsidy to importers. So the heating bill for that building is $175,000. If that oil were paid at the international price it would cost after deductions $134,375 more, that is $309,375 for heating that building.
Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, that building is very close to five wood waste burners. A simple calculation has shown that one tonne of dry chips is equivalent, as far as energy is concerned, to three barrels of oil. So that establishment would use about 2,000 tonnes of chips a year, the energy equivalent at prevailing prices would be $84 a tonne of dry chips and almost twice that if the cost of oil were estimated at the international price. You will ask me: do we have in the northwest enough chips to heat that building? 1 mentioned 2,000 tonnes of chips a year for that building.
At the Department of Lands and Forests, in Abitibi, I was assured that natural reforestation represents 1,676,000 cunits. For the laymen, a cunit is 100 cubic feet. It is the equivalent of a cut forest of coniferous trees. In fact, the forest regenerates entirely. One thing is difficult to find: that cut wood represents 55 per cent of the tree. So, to cut 1,676,000 cunits you must cut a volume of trees of three million cunits. Those three million cunits are made up of 12 per cent chips which makes 360,000 cunits of chips. Those volumes have a weight of about 500,000 tonnes which represent, as I said earlier, three barrels of oil per tonne. So, the chips we produce in Abitibi are the equiva-
November 25, 1980

lent of 1.5 million barrels of oil every year. Furthermore, such energy losses cost us $32 million in oil imports at today's prices. And that, Mr. Speaker, is only the bark; 33 per cent of the tree is still left in the bush.
I am pleased that the government is aiming at energy self-sufficiency by 1990. The example I have given clearly proves there are huge wastes of energy. The CF1IP program is oil conservation legislation. The conversion of heating systems, particularly in my constituency, and the incentives to do it, that is up to $800, is a step aimed at reducing our oil consumption. I leave it to my colleagues to deal with the other benefits of the national energy program.
Mr. Speaker, 1 do not want to go on and on in my maiden speech in the House. I thank you again for allowing me to rise in this debate. This proclamation could have been avoided if an agreement on oil pricing had been possible with the main producing province. I feel, however, that an agreement might be reached before long. However, we must go forward in order to achieve energy self-sufficiency. I hope that these brief remarks on one aspect only of the energy program will bring home to us here, in Canada, our lack of concern about conserving this valuable energy.

Mr. Speaker, this debate is on the Petroleum Administration Act. I think we ought to analyse it to some extent and consider what in fact is happening.
First of all I should like to refer to section 22(2) which reads as follows:
An agreement for the purpose of this part need not be expressed in any formal document executed on behalf of the parties thereto if the expression of that agreement is contained in reciprocal orders in council issued by the governments concerned.
Mr. Speaker, last December 11 the Conservative government of the day presented a budget which set out the details of an energy agreement. That energy agreement would have been confirmed by orders in council had the budget been passed. The agreement would have been in accordance with the provisions of the Petroleum Administration Act. Members on the government side today say "show me the agreement." Sir, the agreement was expressed and shown to them on December 11. It was not completed in accordance with section 22 of the act simply because the government was defeated and an election called. The government did not feel it proper to go through the order in council procedure with the government of Alberta to complete a deal under the Petroleum Administration Act. Members opposite talk about an agreement and the ability to reach an agreement. Sir, there was an agreement. That agreement would have been reduced to order in council in accordance with the act. Of course it could not have been because of the defeat of the government on December 13. Throughout the election campaign we were criticized for the terms of that agreement.
Petroleum Administration Act
What happened during that period? When that agreement was made the price of oil on the international market was approximately $22 U.S. per barrel. Today it is approximately $30 to $32 U.S. a barrel in the Persian Gulf. And what has happened about the 18 cents a gallon? Well, it was 21.9 cents per litre for gasoline in my riding in December of 1979. It is now November, 1980, and the price is 29.9 cents per litre. That is 8 cents more per litre. There are 4.5 litres to a gallon and by my figuring the price of gasoline has gone up 36 cents under this government so far this year.
We talk about agreements. The concept of the Petroleum Administration Act is that effort should be made to obtain agreement between the producing province and the federal government. This calls into question the nature of the effort to obtain an agreement. There were virtually no discussions of consequence between the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and the minister of energy in the legislature of Alberta during this period. Not until July 25 did the minister of energy from this House decided to have one more meeting. I point out that there have been no meetings since July 25 with the government of Alberta. The old agreement under the existing act expired on June 30. We have been without an agreement since that time. There has been no honest effort by the minister of energy or the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to come to grips with the making of an agreement. We are now faced with the enactment of section 35 of the Petroleum Administration Act whereby this government is telling us that it cannot get an agreement. Mr. Speaker, ministers over there have an obligation to demonstrate to this House and to the people of Canada that they have tried.
We have all had the opportunity of seeing Premier Lough-eed on television telling us about the letter he wrote three weeks before the budget was handed down asking for another meeting. There has yet to be a meeting between the minister of energy and the Premier of Alberta, or a meeting between the Prime Minister of this country and the Premier of Alberta. Indeed, the Prime Minister has spent more time negotiating with the President of Mexico, Mr. Portillo, and Sheik Yamani than he has with the Premier of Alberta. He is more interested in dealing with the Mexicans and the Arabs than he is with the Premier of Alberta or, indeed, the Premier of Saskatchewan. He has made no honest effort to come to an agreement.
I would like to speak for a moment about this Mexican deal. What do we get from it? He went around talking about the great deal with Mexico. Well, it is a deal that will aggravate marketing of heavy oil to the point where we will have difficulty in refining it. It imposes significant cost burdens on Canadians and Canadian consumers. We are paying an outrageous price for this oil, a price far in excess of what we get for selling equivalent heavy oil, produced in the Lloydminster fields, to the United States. This is difficult oil to refine; it has a high sulphur content. We are buying it at world price plus, yet we cannot even sell our own heavy oil produced in Lloydminster and other fields in the west. Indeed, some of those fields are prorated down to 50 per cent. That is the type of oil

November 25, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act
deal we have had. That is the kind of effort we have seen to make an agreement-agreements with Mexicans but no agreements with Canadians. What is being said through this act to the people of Canada is: "I cannot make a deal". Well, the Prime Minister has not tried. He has not wanted to.
I could talk about other deals they made with foreigners. Specifically, they made a deal with Roumania back in 1972. They bought 100,000 barrels of oil which was so poor that it could not be refined. They could not burn it, or use it. Whatever happened to that oil we do not know. What have we seen in terms of negotiations with the Prime Minister, the sheik of sheiks, who is going around the world trying to make deals but who is really not honestly trying to put together compromises that will make an energy policy?
I am very pleased to see the Minister of State for Multicul-turalism (Mr. Fleming) is here tonight since I want to talk about the philosophy of this government and I want to refer to the speech he made to the Canadian Club in Vancouver, British Columbia, on November 12, 1980. I refer the minister to page 11 of his speech and 1 intend to quote the whole paragraph, which reads:
Until the energy crisis, the provinces had almost a free hand in exporting resources as they saw fit. Ottawa didn't want to stand-didn't even appear to want to stand-in the way of western development. It didn't want to weaken national unity while separatism was gaining ground in Quebec. Nor could it afford a confrontation with the combined power of the provinces, the multinationals, and the government of the United States. And power unused is power abdicated.
Who are our enemies? The minister says that the provinces are our enemies. The minister says number two enemy is the multinationals and enemy number three of the government is the government of the United States. That is the way in which this government approaches national unity. Their number one enemy is the provinces. And this is the minister talking, sir, a man who is a representative of the government and of government policy here. Their number two enemy is the multinationals and enemy number three is the government of the United States. "And power unused is power abdicated." That is what this act is all about. Power unused is power abdicated and "- confrontation with the combined power of the provinces, the multinationals-" is what the minister refers to. I would like to read another paragraph from that speech:
Clearly, the federal government has lost some credibility. But if it can be blamed for Canada's problems, it's not for asserting too much control but too little; not for too much confrontation but too much accommodation.
Where is the accommodation?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
speechtext: Read the whole speech.

Mr. Speaker, 1 read his whole speech. The hon. minister can speak later and explain it. When he talks about confrontation that is the-policy of this government.
The policy of the government is to beat down the provinces and the companies which have been trying to develop this country. That is the reason the Petroleum Administration Act was proclaimed. It is not for want of agreement, but for want
of confrontation, because that is the way in which the government approaches, and has always approached, such issues. I first spoke on this matter in 1973 during debate on a bill to bring about the Energy Supplies Emergency Act. I spoke in this House on December 12, 1973. While preparing for this debate I thought I would take a look at what I had already said in this House with respect to energy, so I dug up that speech. I was most interested in some of the remarks contained therein, and I would like to quote from my own speech.
Oh, God!
Are you that hard up for material?

Perhaps some members of the New Democratic Party were here at the time, but most of them were not because they do not last long in this House. I would like to quote from page 8690 of Hansard of December 12, 1973:
The government does not really care about those provinces. It has simply told them what it intends to do: it has operated on a principle of confrontation.
Mr. Speaker, in a situation like that, when one person declares unilaterally that he will tax the resources of your province, the next thing that happens is that the person who has been treated in this fashion acts, or reacts, in the same fashion. It is impossible to develop a spirit of community in Canada on the basis of the concept of two lawyers engaged in a lawsuit, or of two businessmen competing with each other at an auction. This whole atmosphere of confrontation in dominion-provincial relations, is one which ought to arise and did not arise before this Prime Minister became Liberal leader. This has been the climate over the past four years and it is about time it changed because it is not doing Canada any good.
1 will not read my entire speech. My friend for Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski) was here and he will remember his comments. I went on to say at page 8691:
If we continue to tweak their noses, and continue to push the interests of central Canada against the resource provinces, we are not going to keep confederation together-and that is a pretty serious matter.
I made those remarks in 1973, and since that time the government has continued to carry on in that fashion. It is no wonder there is no agreement. Its policy is confrontation and further confrontation. What has happened since 1973? We eventually arranged the passage of the Petroleum Administration Act and there was agreement for $1 half yearly increases in oil prices. A portion of that increase went to the federal government, 45 per cent went to the provinces and 45 per cent to the companies. It became apparent early in 1979 that it was necessary to renegotiate that deal.
As a result of that necessity to renegotiate, the Clark government proceeded through the summer and fall of 1979 to renegotiate the deal and settlement which became the subject of the Crosbie budget of December 11. The question is, could we have continued with the negotiations this year which were terminated as a result of the defeat of the Crosbie budget and as a result of the fact that the arrangement under section 22 of the Petroleum Administration Act could not be completed.
Ronald Anderson in his column in the Toronto Globe and Mail recently reported that a company called Data Resources of Canada has suggested the probability of a compromise does exist, that a compromise can be reached. Compromise is essential to this whole question of dominion-provincial rela-
November 25, 1980

tions, of fairness and of the way in which one part of Canada perceives the tax levied on its resources. The suggestion in the article is that while Alberta has been asking for a $4.50 increase in the price of oil, under the current split in increases the province would probably reduce that claim to approximately $3.25 per barrel. Indeed, the Premier of Alberta indicated that he sees no reason why oil prices in Canada should be any more than 75 per cent of the world price, to be phased in over a period of time.
There have been all sorts of efforts at compromise, but because this government perceives the provinces, the companies and the United States as its enemies, these efforts have not been effective. When I spoke in the House in 1973 this country was a net exporter of oil. The problem then was moving oil from our surplus region in western Canada to our deficit regions in eastern Canada. It was difficult to move oil then because there were no pipelines or other systems of easy delivery to the east.
It was also apparent in 1973 that Canada had to become self-sufficient in oil because OPEC had been organized and oil prices had escalated to $4 a barrel. These events were seen to be disastrous. Of course, prices have escalated many times since, but at that point we understood the potential of the tar sands and what could be done. We knew that in the bituminous sands of the west there was buried heavy oil-more oil than in the whole of Arabia. At that time the government of Alberta along with Imperial Oil and other companies put together the Syncrude project. It was suggested that instead of a royalty they would take 50 per cent of the profits. It was suggested by the then leader of the New Democratic Party that there probably would not be any profits from the Syncrude project for a long time and that the province of Alberta would get very little out of it. All of this has happened since 1973, and 18 months ago the Syncrude project came onstream. However, there have been no further projects of that nature since.
As a nation, we have really done nothing to mobilize the resources of our country. We have witnessed confrontation and fights, but there has been no need for these antics. We have the greatest land in the world and resources which are unmatched by any other country. We have long known about our potential oil resources in the north, but we have not taken a single drop of those resources to market. We have known about the gas reserves in the north, but again, none of that gas has gone to market. Again, we have had nothing but regulation, confrontation and the government going after the multinationals because they are bad boys-they might conceivably make a profit and we might become self-sufficient.
Mr. Speaker, we could become self-sufficient and we should be self-sufficient now. The tragedy is that we have left it so late. If it was to take ten years to be self-sufficient, we should have started in 1973. The crime is the responsibility of competing governments, particularly of this government which views as its enemies, the provinces, the multinationals and the United States. It is unfortunate we should wind up with this kind of attitude. Look at the way this government views one
Petroleum Administration Act
company which some years ago experimented in the tar sands. That company was called The Great Canadian Oil Sands. It has since amalgamated and been renamed Suncor. It is largely foreign owned by Sun Oil Company which owns 98 per cent of it. It is a multinational company and therefore an enemy of the government. But that company invested and built the technology on which we can now rely for oil self-sufficiency in the tar sands development. How does this government treat that company? It says to that company, to the explorer, the developer of the technology, "You are no better than any other Joe who drills an easy well. The price of your oil is $16.75-or whatever-a barrel. That is what you get. Ycu do not get the $38 plus change and the CPI on top which your competitor Syncrude gets or any other person who goes into developing heavy oil or tar sands recovery. You have done all the work. You have developed all the technology but you will not get the price because that is the way we treat the risk investors. Besides you are a dirty multinational and enemy number two." They are not enemy number one. Enemy number two is good enough, but maybe they could be enemy number three because their head office is located in the United States.
There are all sorts of possibilities in this country in terms of energy development. We hear from this side about the lack of employment for people in the north, the lack of employment for native people, and so on. How will we ever put people to work if we do not develop the resources we have, resources capable of putting them to work? How can we put them to work? What do we do? Do we put them on welfare forever? Can we not put people to work? Can we not give people opportunities to be part of this world in this century? Would hon. members rather pay these people off? Do they want to look after them in the welfare cage forever? That is the NDP attitude. That is the attitude which says our enemies are the multinationals, the United States and the provinces. That is the attitude of the confrontation which this group to my left, the red rump of the group over there, would like to develop and push on. The hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) talked about making sure the private companies do something. Then he stopped and said he had said something wrong; he meant public companies. He knows perfectly well that public companies will never produce anything really worth while. They never have before, nor will they in the future.
1 do not normally repeat what I have said on other occasions in this House but I have talked about some of the things we should be doing. We have the potential for being energy producers and energy exporters of petroleum and natural gas. But what do we do? We do not use that potential to negotiate tariff reductions with the United States. The U.S. is our enemy. We just sell that country natural gas at whatever price we can get. But we do not use the ability to negotiate to make sure that we sell plastics, oil in tin cans and all the things one can make with the resins from the petrochemical industry.
We have a concept that it is wrong to make a profit. I do not know of any successful business yet-that did not make a

November 25, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act
profit. A profit is the motivating force behind doing something. If people organized in a business do not make that activity profitable, they will not do it. If people are asked to invest their money and they do not see a return on it, they will not make that investment. These fellows over here do not understand that, Mr. Speaker. Presumably the government does not understand it either. Presumably the government is going to make sure it is not profitable to be in the oil business. In other words, the government is going to make sure it will be exceedingly unprofitable to do so.
I shall read a short letter which was delivered to the Minister of Finance. It came from a small oil company in Alberta called Gladstone Petroleum Ltd. and it reads:
I am forwarding under separate cover to the provincial government, applications to abandon six oil wells. This decision to abandon oil wells has been made necessary due to the onerous taxes and royalties to which have been added the terms of the presently proposed budget.
Admittedly, these wells are marginal, each capable of yielding 40 to 60 barrels of light gravity oil per month. In a favourable royalty, taxation, and pricing climate, these wells could operate at cost, or at slight profit.
That is the kind of attitude this budget has presented to these small companies. They say to themselves, "Better that we do not invest our money." Or else they say, "We cannot make any profit pumping 40 to 60 barrels a month from a well which costs a lot to operate. It is better to turn off the taps and not doing anything." That is the incentive given under the pricing system imposed under this act. The refusal, the unwillingness and the absolute disregard for the interests of the provinces and the people involved in the oil industry in determining the price formula demanded under this proclamation are what is wrong with the proclamation.
The concept has been developed in the ivory towers here in Ottawa by people far away from drilling rigs. These people over in the EMR building, the Taj Mahal, are the ones who have figured out what they think is a proper rate of return for someone going into a risky business, what they think they can get away with in terms of an imposed pricing structure. But this attitude is not working. Companies are abandoning exploration and development opportunities. Companies have decided they cannot make enough money here, so they will go somewhere else. Members from this side of the House talk about rigs leaving Canada. They know about it because they happen to come from western Canada. They talk about the industry not going ahead the way it should. We all know the industry is not going the way it should. We all know that under this government there has been no new tar sands project started since Syncrude. We all know that no new development has gone on.
The efforts of this government have been directed to the Sheik Yamanis or the Portillos. Those are the kinds of people with whom this government wants to negotiate. It does not want to negotiate and settle with Canadians.
Thank Exxon.

We have a situation where productivity in this country this year has declined 3.3. per cent on the basis of individuals employed. While employment has gone up 2 per
cent, we are producing 1.1 per cent or 1.2 per cent gross less goods and services this year than we did last. In other words, we are employing more people this year to produce less goods and services. Yet there is opportunity to make this country great. We have the resources. We know there is a world out there demanding our petroleum and gas resources and the chemicals we can produce from them. All of this means employment for Canadians. When we have 8 per cent of Canadians unemployed-and maybe more pretty soon-and when businesses are slowing down and there is a drop in productivity, something is wrong.
I want to mention a concern that I and others have with respect to what is happening in Canada and the effect the invocation of the Petroleum Administration Act has on the unity of this country.
Normally speaking, an ordinary statute setting the price of a commodity would not cause much concern. However, we have witnessed a period of constitutional debate and increased concern about oil, oil pricing and resource policy. On top of that, we have seen the unilateral imposition of a pricing formula which is clearly not satisfactory to any of the producing provinces or even the potential producing provinces.
As a result, when speaking in this House, my colleagues have said there is a bit of a prairie fire developing in western Canada. That prairie fire has been fanned by a confrontation attitude on the part of this government. It is not the first time a prairie fire has developed there. Members of this House will realize that at one point the old line parties-an expression used by my friends to the left-were totally frozen out from the UFO, the progressive movement, the social credit movement and the CCF movement. These political movements developed in western Canada because of true economic reasons.
There is today a political movement developing there, led by many people. I have known for quite a while-and I wish I could call him a friend again-the former leader of the opposition in the province of Saskatchewan, Dick Culver. There are people in politics seriously advocating that a part of this country leave and join the United States or leave and become some other country. That is serious. While the poll taken prior to the budget may have showed only 10 per cent separatist leanings, there was a significant indication of unhappiness and of a feeling that the west could go it alone. As a result of the policies of this government, confirmed in the proclamation of this act, we could very easily wind up with no honest attempt to obtain an agreement. This could cause a disaster, a unity problem and the separation of our country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Simmons (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to see my good friend from Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski) so much in anticipation. I shall not disappoint him. I thank him for coming out tonight, braving the weather, sacrificing to be here. My good friend from Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) is here
November 25, 1980

tonight in body and spirit. I thank him as well. I want to especially thank my good friend from Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). I want to say something to him before he leaves the chamber, as he is about to do, to indulge in one of his weaknesses.
Explain.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
I say to him there was no agreement. He really should not mislead the Canadian people about that. I remind him that a day or so before the budget came down, indeed, I think the day after the Tory budget came down on December 11, a senior governmental official in Alberta said quite candidly and publicly there was no agreement. I know there are those who want to rewrite history and say it was otherwise, but the public record is quite clear that there was no agreement.
I concede to the hon. member they may well have been near an agreement. After all, they are bedfellows, being of the same political stripe. They should have been able to get their heads together, given the seven or eight months they had. However, the hon. member should not mislead the people of Canada by perpetrating this motion of agreement. There was no agreement.
While I have the ear of the hon. member for Mississauga South, may I say he did some rather interesting arithmetic when he talked about the price of gas in his riding last December compared to now. He said it had gone up 32 or 36 cents. He tied that somehow to the Tory gas tax. What he did not tell his listeners was that under the Tory administration, had it continued beyond December 13, the price of gas would have gone up by perhaps an equivalent amount. One can argue about whether it would have gone up 32, 34 or 36 cents, but it would have been roughly an equivalent amount. In addition, there would have been an 18-cent tax on top of that. That is the point he should have made to his listeners.
I thank the hon. member for his wisdom and his arithmetic. The last time he treated the people of Canada to his considerable wisdom, he was telling them what he thought of Canada's native people. As we did not share his views on that subject, we do not share his arithmetic either.
I am told the Chinese have a set of symbols or a word in their language which not only means crisis, but opportunity. They use the same word or set of characters for both crisis and opportunity. There are those who tell us that the oil controversy is reaching a crisis. Whether that is the case or not, it is certainly at the point where it is an opportunity for us to do something in this country that should have been done a long time ago. It is time for some planning and determined action. That is what brings us to "The National Energy Program" tabled in this House two weeks ago.
There are three elements in the program I wish to mention briefly tonight. Before doing so, I want to reflect for a moment on a point I was making in response to the hon. member for Mississauga South. No national government, Liberal or Tory, and I am not deliberately omitting my friends from the NDP,
Petroleum Administration Act
because it is not a worry they have to contend with in the foreseeable future-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: My good friend from Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) is always worth mentioning. We are delighted to see him out this evening. As a matter of fact, the opposition is out in force tonight. There are at least a dozen or 15.
How are you doing over there?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: We are doing very well over here.
Some are, but not you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: No national government, whatever its political stripe, is going to be able to get an agreement easily. The hon. member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) found that out when he was prime minister. He came close, but he did not quite get the agreement. We have reached the conclusion that the time has come, if we intend to build something of a heritage for those who come after us, to cease doing things on an ad hoc basis as far as energy matters are concerned.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member from Come-By-Chance just mentioned that there are a number of members in the House. I do not think he should begin to reflect on the attendance of this House when we have different committees meeting in other places.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. With all due respect to the hon. member for Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski), I think he has made his point.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
I am proud to tell my good friend from Edmonton North that my riding is Burin-St. George's. His good friend from St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) actually represents Come-By-Chance. He will learn that if he stays around long enough.
There are three elements to the program, Mr. Speaker; security of supply, the opportunity for Canadians to participate in the oil industry and some fairness in pricing and revenue sharing. I should like to spend a little time on each of these. I submit they cannot be obtained if we are to depend on OPEC, if we are forced to allow circumstances half way round the world, the vagaries of political life in a politically unstable part of the world, to determine one of the basic economic facts of life here in Canada. If we continue to do that, we are fooling ourselves. We will have difficulty in planning the economic and industrial development of this country. How can a farmer or a fisherman build his enterprise over the next few years if he does not know what the price of oil will be two, three or five years from now?
We are fortunate in this country that we have enough petroleum for our immediate requirements. We do not need to worry of being deprived of winter heating oil because there has been a sudden change of government half way round the globe.
