November 25, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act
In this we are more fortunate than most countries. It would be immoral if we let slip by this marvellous opportunity to plan the energy supply and pricing mechanism for Canada and to secure for our fellow countrymen some measure of security.
The second part of the government's energy program is opportunity, opportunity for Canadians to participate in the energy industry. It is difficult to achieve this as long as the greater part of our gas and oil industry is under foreign control and ownership. These resources are finite and they are the heritage of the people of Canada. The federal and provincial governments are the custodians, the trustees of that particular heritage. The people of this country should in the end be the prime beneficiaries of the resources of the oil industry. As long as the greater part of this country's oil and gas industry remains foreign owned and foreign dominated, that is impossible.
The foreign companies export capital from this country at an alarming rate. Between 1975 and 1979 the total outflow of capital was $3.7 billion. That is a monstrous transfer of wealth from Canada to foreign shareholders. It is a state of affairs tolerated by no other nation in the world.
Ten million dollars?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
I know my friend for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) might not want to hear this because his party has adopted the position of being the spokesman for the multinationals. I know the truth is hard to bear but this has to be said. I say to him, this outflow of capital has to stop.
I am not surprised that the oil companies have begun to squirm, that the large multinationals have reacted so violently to the national energy program. This does not surprise me at all because our proposal means they will not make quite as many dollars as in the past. They can afford to cut back on their profits. For example, for the six months ending August 18, 1980, Gulf Canada's net income rose 74 per cent; for the second quarter of 1980 it rose 76 per cent to $95 million.
Is that an isolated example, Mr. Speaker? Let us look at Imperial Oil. Their income rose 52 per cent. What about BP Canada? I promise my friends in the NDP I am not going to mention Husky Oil tonight. I have too much respect for my good friend Tommy Douglas. I am talking about the companies the other opposition party supports.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the net income of BP Canada for the six months ended June 30, 1980, more than doubled to over $59 million. That is the group the hon. member for Mississauga South defends. That is the group he is worried about lest they slip back from $59 million to $58 million or $57 million. What nonsense! Of course, the multinationals are going to squirm, they are going to react. They are going to lay out their public relations millions. They are going to put the steamroller into action to see if they can stop all opposition to anything but the carte blanche they have been given in this country for too many years.
The third part of the national energy program is the thrust for fairness, fairness in pricing-
Oh, oh!

speechtext: -fairness in revenue sharing. The present distribution of revenue from oil and gas is 45 per cent for the provinces, 45 per cent for the oil industry and 10 per cent for the national government.
Who owns it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Who owns it, the member asks. The people of Canada own it, the same people who own this government, the same people who sent the members to this Parliament. We are not owned by the multinationals. We do not have to bow to the multinationals. We do have to bow to respect the wishes of the people of Canada and we make no apologies for that, Mr. Speaker. The federal government bears the financial brunt of the exercise
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
The federal government does bear the financial brunt of the exercise of financing the tax expenditures. The national government has borne 63 per cent of the costs of exploration programs. The Canadian taxpayer has underwritten 63 per cent of the cost of these programs. The federal government, representing all Canadians, has an obligation to cushion regions from the sudden effects of price rises and fuel shortages. These activities are expensive and they must be paid for. What we are doing is not unlike what is being done in many other countries. This afternoon the Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan) drew attention to the situation in Australia and United States, where the state administration or the provincial administration is receiving far less under the programs in these countries than is the case under the national energy program.
This government recognizes that while resources must be utilized for the benefit of all citizens in this country the first claim on the benefit of these resources must be by the people who live in the provinces where the resources are located. It is not the intention of the national energy program to increase the federal government's share substantially at the expense of the provincial treasuries involved but rather to do so at the expense of the multinationals. For that we make no apology.
I wish to speak now on fairness in pricing. Why should the price of oil be determined by OPEC in circumstances that are completely beyond our control? Why this sudden urge to pay world prices for a commodity we produce in this country? Where is the precedent for it? Does this mean we should rush out and pay the world price for other items? If we found the Arabs were paying $2 for a litre of milk, does that mean we too should pay $2 for a litre of milk? Should we not say instead, what does it cost to produce a litre of milk and what is a reasonable return on the investment? Should we not add
November 25, 1980

these two figures together so as to determine a consumer price? That is the way we do it.
That is the way we are determining the price of oil in this country. We are asking what it costs to produce and what is a fair return on investment in the first place. Add those two together, and you will have our price of oil this year, next year and five years down the road. It seems eminently sensible to me that we should arrive at the price of a commodity based on what it costs to produce that commodity, keeping in mind that the person who invests the dollars to produce the commodity should get a reasonable return on his or her investment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is what the people voted for in the last election.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
What has been the practice in this country when the world price of a commodity shoots dramatically upward or dramatically downward? That is a fair question. What has been the practice when the price of wheat, copper or oil has shot dramatically upward or downward? Let us consider those three examples, oil, copper and wheat. What have we been doing?
Is this made-in-Canada price for oil about which we are talking some new scheme we have cooked up over here to aggravate the Alberta government and the oil companies?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: I know that is what the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) would like to believe, but what he believes is not necessarily true, as I found out from reading his Householder which I tripped over getting out of the elevator this morning in the Confederation Building. Having read it, I say to the hon. member instructively that I did not understand hate mail until I saw that Householder. It is a terrible piece of stuff. Should my tax dollars be financing that?
That's all right. We pay for yours.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Hon. members may ask which governments were in power between 1960 and 1973. There were three, a Tory government under Mr. Diefenbaker and a couple of different Liberal administrations, one under Mr. Pearson and one under the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
Under three separate administrations of two party stripes from 1960 to 1973 all of Canada west of the Ottawa River paid about a 25 per cent premium on oil in order to protect Alberta against low oil prices outside this country. There is a precedent. This administration and two or three before it have cushioned Canadians against the effect of dramatically changing prices of oil on the international stage. In the example I gave it was a case where the price of oil went dramatically down, or at least below levels required to continue the production of oil in Canada on an economic basis.
Petroleum Administration Act
For another example why not look at 1969 when international copper prices rose sharply? What was the action taken of the federal government of the day then, led by the same gentleman who leads it today? The federal government kept the Canadian price low and restrained exports to ensure sufficient supplies for Canadian consumers. That is a precedent in the copper industry for what we are doing with the oil industry today.
Do hon. members want a further example which again relates particularly to the western provinces? In 1969 international prices for wheat dropped drastically. The federal government legislated a price higher than world prices to protect the western farmer with regard to grain sold in Canada. The price was higher because the international price dropped so drastically.
Those are just three examples involving parties of two different stripes in government and initiatives which those administrations took to cushion Canadians against rapidly rising or falling prices, as the circumstance may be. These are examples which go back a full 20 years. What we are talking about is not particularly new or novel.
Who will benefit? Let us suppose for the purpose of my argument that tomorrow morning the price of oil were allowed to rise to world levels.
What does Canada charge the United States and the world?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Who would benefit? The multinational oil companies would certainly benefit. Their profits would go up more tens of percentage points, and that would make the official opposition happy, but it would not make me very happy. It would not make my constituents very happy.
They have enough problems with taxes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Of course the oil companies would be happy, but we have not been sent here, and I have not been sent here, to represent multinational oil companies. I do not make any apologies to them. It surprises me that the official opposition spends so much time defending multinational oil companies.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: That is a crock of crude.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) has come in.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: I just woke up.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: It looks as though he has had an interesting evening. He has obviously dined well.
It doesn't look like you are exactly starving.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
I remember when my good friend from Yellowhead was elected leader of the Tory party. The following week a national news magazine, Macleans, had printed across the front cover "Joe Who?" The accompanying article went on to raise some questions about who this new leader was and what he stood for. During the last few weeks when there

Petroleum Administration Act
has been this energy controversy it has become clear what "Joe Who What" means.
It means "Joe XX". The unknown. Those are the two Xs in Exxon. Joe Exxon.
Who gave them S40 million?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
He represents the multinationals. He is the unwitting spokesman, together with his band of Tories, for the multinationals. We heard tonight from the hon. member for Mississauga South. He was quite blatant about it. Most Tories are much more coy in the way they put forward representations on behalf of those companies, but the hon. member for Mississauga South at least deserves credit for being frank and up front about it. If we read the transcript of his address, we will find he was exactly that, very up front about his support for what I think he termed the "poor multinationals" at one point.
We know the multinationals will benefit, but who else will benefit? What about the millwright out in Drayton Valley Alberta, the welder in Brooks, Alberta or the pipefitter out there? Will he benefit if the price of oil now being produced at $16.50 a barrel were to shoot up to $38 a barrel tomorrow morning? How would he benefit? Would the companies rush to the unions and say, "We are going to double the rate for that man"? Would we suddenly see him get twice as much per hour for his work?
He would have to go back to Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: What would it mean to that worker? Would he pay more for items from the plastics industry which he has to purchase? Would he pay more for gas for his car? Would he pay more for food from the farm because of increased farm prices which would be the result of increased oil prices? The answers are yes, yes and yes. He would pay more. His cost of living would go up if oil prices went up. But let us not suggest for a minute that that welder or that pipefitter would suddenly get more money. Let us not be so naive to think that the companies would rush in and say, "Mr. Union Leader, we want to negotiate a new agreement; your man is not getting enough."
He might be able to keep his job.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: He might hang on to his job, and he might get as much as he is getting now, but the "might" that he would get a little more is a pretty long "might". He would have to work pretty hard. His union would have to do some very tough bargaining before it would convince those "poor" multinationals that somehow a doubling of the price ought to be reflected in his paycheque. Who would benefit? The multinationals.
Should we pay more to Saudi Arabian workers?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
I ask the hon. member in the official opposition who is shouting now to bear with me. When I am finished, he can rise and answer that question himself. Who would
benefit, other than the multinationals, if the price of oil suddenly went up? What is all this shouting and screaming about rushing out tomorrow morning and declaring the world price for oil? What would be the benefit for the constituents these members are supposed to be representing in this chamber?
Isn't the purpose of this act to raise the price of oil?
Isn't that the purpose of this proclamation?
The Liberals want to raise the price to the world price; that is what they are saying.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Who is delaying the Alsands project and the Cold Lake project? Let me talk about those projects for a moment. The federal government is not delaying these two projects.
That is nonsense, absolute nonsense!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: I wish the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) were here tonight. I read the speech he made last night with great interest. Also I read the comments he made in Fort McMurray last Friday night. The disappointing thing is that he did not say in the chamber last night what he said in Fort McMurray last Friday before his constituents. He made two contradictory statements, and I invite him to correct the record on that. Before his constituents in Fort McMurray he indicated what I just said a moment ago, that it was not the fault of the Government of Canada that these projects have not proceeded. He laid the blame squarely upon the government of Alberta.
Say that again.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
I will say some more things which might clarify the point for the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson). I refer to a Canadian Press story published a couple of days ago. It reads as follows:
Cold Lake businessmen want Alberta Premier Peter Lougheed to let Imperial Oil Ltd.'s $9-billion Cold Lake heavy oil project proceed.
They ask Premier Lougheed to let the project proceed. I am sure it is clear who is stopping it in the minds of the businessmen of Cold Lake. It is not this government, but the government of Alberta.
Perhaps I should refer to a recent editorial which appeared in The Edmonton Sun, a paper which has not been known to agree with everything the government has done in the energy field, but which nevertheless calls unequivocally on the Alberta government to stop delaying the projects. In part it reads:
There is simply nothing to be gained by such an approach. The megaplants will not produce oil of any quantity to speak of until 1987, long after the current energy war. The plants will thus have no immediate impact on oil supplies to eastern Canada.
Mr. Lougheed's stance on the plants is totally punitive and totally negative.
November 25, 1980

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired. He may continue only with the unanimous consent of the House.

Mr. Speaker, the speech we have just heard was very interesting and entertaining. After hearing it I think I finally understand the Liberal policy on energy. Basically they are very strong socialists and very strong nationalists when it comes to the empty wells, but they believe in subsidizing the multinationals when it comes to the full wells.
Hear, hear!

A number of areas in Canada will be adversely affected by the government's energy decision. The government has refused to recognize the effects of its energy policies on the north. Last month in northern Manitoba, in the constituency of Churchill which I represent, there was a 29 per cent increase by Steelgas which provides the gas for most northern Manitoba communities. This happened before the budget increase. It is owned and supplied by Dome Petroleum. Dome Petroleum will not give us its cost figures in setting the price to its wholly-owned subsidiary.
There was another action in the last couple of weeks, with CN Express announcing that it will be closing down its operations which will increase the cost of food and other items going to northern communities. Food is already flown into many isolated communities in northern Canada. The higher cost of fuel increases the cost of each and every good to those communities. There are communities in my constituency where gas already costs over $5 per gallon. In other northern communities the price of gas and other items is even higher.
I read with interest an article which appeared in The Globe and Mail earlier this week. It pointed out that the Port Severn Indians, most of whom are on some form of welfare, pay $2.22 for a dozen eggs, as compared to $1.29 in Toronto; $4.02 for two kilograms of sugar which sell for only $2.49 in Toronto; $1.57 for a loaf of bread which costs 80 cents in Toronto; $3.44 for a pound of hamburger which costs $1.98 in Toronto; $1.75 for a fresh quart of milk which costs only 75 cents in Toronto. The price of goods in northern communities is extremely high.
In Saskatchewan the provincial government implemented a program of subsidizing the shipment of these foods into northern communities. The federal government has no program for its northern residents. The cost of transportation over the long distances involved has worked against industrial development in each and every one of those communities. This was the situation prior to the budget.
Now we must add the increased cost of energy imposed by the government, not because of any increase in the cost of production, but because the Liberal government, like its Tory predecessor, is increasing prices in order to enrich its own coffers and those of the multinationals. As the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) said, it might be a smaller slice but it is a much larger pie. The multinationals
Petroleum Administration Act
will benefit from the budget, even without the blackmail and the strikes we hear about in the press at this time. Because the government is weak by nature and by tradition, it will give in to the multinationals eventually. The history of the Walter Gordon budget and the entire Liberal machine has been to talk tough but to carry a very small stick.
Hear, hear!

No consideration was given to the increased costs of living faced by the residents of northern communities. There were no new programs. There were no new subsidies to help low-income natives and other Canadians who live in isolated areas. There were no programs to compensate for the high cost of running a business in the north. Steelgas, the Dome controlled and owned company about which I spoke earlier, after receiving a 29 per cent increase three weeks ago, is asking for another one.
Throughout the west there is dissent because of what the government has presented in the budget and the energy package. In return for losing potential revenue, the west received a western development fund. It is the old story-the Liberal government takes away with one hand and gives with the other. What does the west receive? It receives a $4-billion fund, of which only $2 billion will be given in three years; no date was given for the other $2 billion. It will be a program controlled by Ottawa bureaucrats. There are no guidelines to ensure that these funds will be used for needed development. There are no guidelines to prove that this money will not be used just to replace existing federal funds which go to the west. There are no guidelines to ensure that the minister responsible-not the minister responsible for DREE, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane), but the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy)-will not use this fund as a slush fund to rebuild the Liberal party in western Canada. When there is $4 billion for economic development in the country, it should be used where it is needed. The guidelines should be set by Parliament, and as the DREE committee unanimously agreed, it should be under the control and co-ordination of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration loves to make controversial remarks, only because he needs the press. Last week he was out west and he said that Liberals are born-again westerners. I cannot find anyone in my constituency who evens admits to being a Liberal. If hon. members opposite were born-again westerners, they would not have issued this energy proclamation. It would never have taken place because they would understand the resentment and the hatred which they are provoking by this kind of action. I will talk more about the west later.
Right now I would like to talk about the impact of the energy program on the Atlantic provinces. Prices are traditionally higher in the Atlantic provinces. Prices of oil and gas are higher whether or not there is a subsidy. The prices of goods in

November 25, 1980
Petroleum Administration Act
those communities are higher. The prices of goods shipped to those communities are higher. Communities in the Atlantic provinces are not eligible for the conversion subsidy which other provinces will receive if people convert from oil to gas heating. This region was discriminated against because it was supposed that a number of oil fired generators were being used and, therefore, the program would not save people or the federal government any oil. It would save some in the other provinces. This does not mean that people in Atlantic Canada should not benefit from a program like this. Those people will have to pay the higher costs of oil and gas. They should benefit from a program of this nature.
In addition, the Liberals, as usual, did not get their facts straight. New Brunswick does not qualify for this program yet if you look at the facts you will find that only two of their eight power stations presently use oil as a source of energy- only two. What happened to the Liberal members of Parliament from New Brunswick? Were they quiet? Did they not have any influence on their government? Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, of those two power stations one is in the process of being converted to coal at the present time. So in the future seven of the eight power stations will be using coal, hydro power or nuclear power. But the people in New Brunswick will not qualify for this conversion program.
Obviously in setting their budget, as in setting their energy policy, this government did not know what it was doing. Statistics will illustrate that for every dollar increase in the price of oil there is a 1 per cent increase in the rate of inflation. Inflation is already higher in the maritime provinces than it is in the rest of Canada. This energy package will only increase the cost of living for people in that region.
The national energy policy said some nice things about the future of the Atlantic region. I would like to quote:
As for opportunity, the Atlantic region, long disadvantaged in a number of ways, stands on the verge of an energy boom-oil and gas, electricity and coal-that could provide the basis for a new sustainable prosperity. The national energy program can-and does-provide the framework to ensure that this happens.
Those were lovely words but if you take a look at the energy program they are hard to believe. Things do not happen for the Atlantic region, they happen to the Atlantic region. As I said, unemployment there is already high but with higher energy costs it will only increase. The cost of living is higher. The cost of heating is higher. The cost of transportation is higher. And as a result of this national energy policy those costs will double by 1984.
What will happen with respect to regional economic development? Nothing. There is no co-ordination by the minister responsible for DREE because the cabinet will not give him that power. There is half an effort to do something for that region through the industrial tax credit but that will not work very well for a number of reasons. The most promising industries like lumber, fishing and farming are excluded from benefiting from this tax credit.
As I mentioned in an earlier speech, this program was implemented retroactive to the night of the tabling of the budget. Even though it is supposed to be a tax incentive plan to
attract industry into the Atlantic regions and other parts of Canada which are so designated, it is retroactive to the night of the tabling of the budget. Obviously, companies which were already building in the Atlantic region on October 28 and 29, November 1 and 2, did not come to the Atlantic region because of this tax incentive. For those corporations it is strictly another rip-off. That tax incentive will be given to every corporation which develops in various regions of Canada that are designated, regardless of need and regardless of other subsidies they may be receiving. In other words, if you look at what was supposed to be an effort at regional economic expansion you will find another tax rip-off by the very same people who are now talking in such strong socialist and national tones. Again, the words sound nice but when you examine the actions you find there is nothing there. More important, any positive effects which would have taken place because of the industrial tax credit will be nullified by the huge increases in energy costs predicted in this program. A corporation that is considering developing in the Atlantic will not come in if it knows that its cost of energy will double in the next four years and rise even higher after that. Any benefit from that tax incentive will just not be there.
I would like to say something now about the western development fund to which I was referring earlier. This $4 billion boondoggle is not for Atlantic Canada yet in the west, with the exception of the province of Manitoba, there are booming economies. There is growth in that region of Canada yet they are to receive this $4 billion. It is amazing that the Liberal government should have decided the Atlantic region does not need that kind of money. In the west there are only two Liberal members of Parliament and the west receives $4 billion. I suspect we now have a new definition of political patronage. It used to be the case that the Liberal government would say in a mild, suggestive manner that it would be really good to have a Liberal MP from your region because it would ensure that money flowed back to those constituencies. With the $4 billion plan the opposite is true. What we now have is a benefit for not voting Liberal-the west is being rewarded for not voting Liberal.
Hear, hear!
Just imagine what $4 billion could have done for Nova Scotia. Imagine what it could have done for New Brunswick, Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island-
Where are their MPs?

Not only that. Where are the cabinet ministers from those regions? I ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Regan), who is unusually quiet today about the effect of higher energy prices on Nova Scotia, what $4 billion could have done for Sysco? I would ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) what $4 billion could have done for Devco, Sysco or other corporations which are in need in Nova Scotia? Can you imagine the benefit if the Minister of Finance had allocated that money to eastern Canada, the provinces that are really in need? We would not find him studying a business plan for
November 25, 1980

Sysco at this time. He would be running out there in order to hand out the cheque, especially with a byelection coming. Well, we in the west have learned our lesson. We found that it pays in many ways not to vote Liberal. The people in Atlantic Canada will be finding out the same thing in the future.
Because of the government's lack of planning the boom they talk about as a result of the national energy program, may not happen. There is no guarantee that the ownership and development of our offshore oils will be Canadian. There is no guarantee that the jobs provided will be for Canadians. Last week the Economic Council of Canada released a report pointing out that offshore exploration does not necessarily mean the Messiah has come.
It will take action by both the federal government and the provincial government to ensure that the people of that region are trained to take the jobs which will be available. My party is on record as saying we believe that offshore resources should be controlled by the provinces. We also recognize that there is a strong need for a federal presence in determining the future of those resources. But that will not come about under the Liberal government because it does not really believe in planning when it gets down to the nitty-gritty, hard-core decisionmaking. It believes in putting out pamphlets, advertising and the glitter of progress, but when we get underneath that shell, we find it is the same old game. The whole country is suffering from the government's lack of policy.
Never has there been a strong energy program in this country. To give an example, I refer to my province of Manitoba where there is great potential for the development of hydroelectricity. Indeed Manitoba has a surplus in this resource. It also has a number of power plants which could be brought on stream in the near future, yet that power goes unused. The federal government, however, is encouraging the people of Manitoba to switch from oil to gas. The program does not allow for the development and use of Manitoba's hydro power. It does not set up a western grid or a grid into Ontario to enable that power to be used; it simply ignores it entirely. The program does not look at the alternative sources which are available and which could be developed in the future.
There is no energy shortage in Canada. There is certainly misuse and underuse of resources. The government has set up a paper tiger, something which it can tackle rather than a program which would tackle the real problems which we face. The New Democratic Party believes that oil prices should go up but only in certain circumstances and only at a gradual rate. It believes there must be a cost of living allowance so that consumers who are hit the hardest would be cushioned against the higher prices. We believe that the extra revenues from increased prices should not go to the multinationals as they would under the present policy, or to the federal-provincial coffers but that they should be put into a special fund which would be set up to look into the alternative energy schemes and innovative ways of providing rapid transit.
Petroleum Administration Act
The NDP also believes in an over-all industrial strategy which must be flexible enough to adapt to any increases in the price of oil and gas. These proposals are not provided for in the Liberal energy program. The Petroleum Administration Act is a last ditch effort by the government to take over the control of resources. The Liberals have failed to try to achieve any agreement with the provinces. Their ability as negotiators is a real problem. The Conservatives might also listen because they are not so good at negotiating themselves or they would still be in power. The Liberals' record of negotiation is a record of failure.
For example, in negotiating the fisheries treaty with the United States, the government was too weak to develop and conclude an agreement. It was well aware that the agreement must be ratified by the U.S. Senate, because it is written in the constitution of that country, but it did not negotiate from a position of strength and say, "If the treaty is ratified, there is something more for you". Instead the government gave them the whole package after one week's negotiation in the hope that the Senate would graciously give us the treaty we wanted.
The same thing happens when the government negotiates with its employees. The government does not know what it wants to do so it delays by making unrealistics offers which only result in increasing the anger of the employees. Had it given some reasonable offers in the first place and had it known what direction it was going to take, there would not be the militancy about which the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) is so concerned today.
Nor could the Liberal government negotiate on the constitution. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) managed to range all ten provincial premiers against him. Those fellows-there are no ladies yet, but there should be one in Nova Scotia soon- particularly the Conservative premiers, had never agreed on anything in their lives until the Prime Minister made his proposal. We recognize that it is not easy to get agreement with the premiers, but I cannot understand how the Prime Minister could not get at least three or four of those premiers to agree with him on his package, which he would then present to the House.
It is not just a matter of arrogance, it is a matter of the lack of negotiating skill. The Prime Minister does not have to be a hard-core, well-trained unionist, but unfortunately he has none of the skills of negotiation, and as a result the government is in a position of confrontation at this time.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: He negotiated an agreement with your leader.

We negotiated, he accepted. For the benefit of my friend, I would also point out that it is not easy to negotiate with each and every premier. Sterling Lyon of Manitoba has the ability to make Ronald Reagan look like a Liberal. The Liberals have failed to present a package to the provinces. Instead of healing the wounds which are tearing this country apart, the Liberals have increased the division. Alberta has found itself on the losing end of the constitutional debate, the budget proposals and now this energy plan.

Petroleum Administration Act
The people of Alberta love Canada just as much as any group in any part of this land, but the government cannot continue to shove things down their throats and expect those people to love and respect it. Just as I suggested that the Liberals did not know how to negotiate on the constitution, they did not know how to negotiate on the energy package and they refused to accept that there are people in western Canada who believe they have a right to some voice as to the future of their resources. The people of the west should be consulted as a part of the negotiations, not treated to the old method of newspaper debating of which the Liberals are so fond.
The Tory party has taken a very destructive attitude toward the constitutional package, and the Liberal party has taken a very destructive attitude in its energy package. They have failed to recognize that there must be some form of national unity and that people must be made to feel good about the way in which they are being treated. Canadians want a united country. They want co-operative federalism as mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) yesterday when he quoted former prime minister Pearson.
Canadians want a government which will rise above the interests of the factions, as prime minister Pearson mentioned so many years ago, but that is not the attitude of the Liberal government today. We recognize that the government has the right and duty to present the federal alternative, but it can only do this if all the people are willing to work together as citizens of a country in which the governments are openly and honestly negotiating with each other, a country in which the federal government can claim to represent all the regions. Imposition of this measure will serve only to divide Canadians. This government must change its mind. It must open up negotiations. It must open up the hearts of Albertans and others in the west. It must really try to bring Canada together.

Mr. Speaker, first I wish to refer to remarks made by the hon. member for Burin-St. George's (Mr. Simmons). I have been fortunate enough to hear him explain the theory of supply and demand twice. The first time I heard him was a week ago at Queen's University. At that time he explained to third-year business students that the theory of taking your costs, adding reasonable profit and calculating your sales price accordingly was all out of the window. These students had spent three years learning this. It was amazing to see the look in their eyes when his theory of taking the cost, adding a reasonable profit and then selling your product for whatever you can gouge out of people hit home. That may come as somewhat of a surprise to members in this House, but I have had the benefit of hearing it once before. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) was there as well. One of the employees of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce left the room during the expose of costs and sales. He could not handle it, but the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and I had to stay and listen.
I was interested to hear the New Democratic Party explain tonight that the Liberals are not supporting the multinationals. Does this mean the $40 million loan has been recalled already? Last week this place handed out $40 million to the multinationals with no strings attached. It was a situation of "here you are. We need you. We are desperate". That is the degree of support for the multinationals.
I was interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy). Apparently he is the spokesman on behalf of the New Democratic Party for Atlantic Canada. I thought the job of spokesman for Atlantic Canada would belong to the most easterly member of Parliament for the New Democratic Party, namely, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent). Apparently if there is no one available from the east, the next best thing is a member who lives close to the water. So the hon. member for Churchill is the spokesman because Churchill is close to Hudson Bay, and in that way he qualifies. I would like to thank the hon. member for Churchill. One cannot dismiss his remarks that quickly. During the course of his remarks he was very careful to endorse theories, such as the energy tax credit and the excess profits tax on companies. He missed the reduced depletion allowances but he remembered the energy bank. These were all policies that our party enunciated in its budget of last December.
During the debate on the Speech from the Throne members of the government side used this House of Commons as a forum to address their speeches to the province of Quebec and to fight the referendum battle in that province. As a result of the policies of this government, we are now faced with unrest in the west. If that unrest is not dealt with, it could reach untenable and unmanageable proportions.
I want to take a few moments now to address my friends in the west and to tell them about the people of Ontario, not central Canada, but Ontario. We are puzzled by the antagonism of the people in the west toward Ontario. We want to know the specific areas of concern. We promise that if these are brought to our attention, we will apply ourselves, correct the wrongs and explain the situation fully. We do not want the current citizens of Ontario blamed for the problems of this government. If members could come with me tomorrow to the tenth concession in my township and tell everyone there that the people in the west are blaming us for the situation, they would not understand. People in my riding are simply engaged in the process of earning a living, bringing up children and being citizens of our community. Our sons, daughters, nephews and nieces and our friends have gone west with our encouragement. The west is part of this country after all. Our friends and relatives now live in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. But they are still our brothers and sisters. If people out there want to blame anyone, let them blame this government, not the people in Ontario.
This Liberal government is not now and has not been for some time representative of Canada. I would suggest to Ontario members in this House that the Liberal government is not representative of the great province of Ontario. You were elected to govern Canada because you had 99 per cent of the
November 25, 1980

vote in one province. You are completely swamped, subjected and impotent-

Mr. Speaker, I would not suggest for a moment that you were swamped, subjected or impotent. This leads to what we call confrontation politics. The hon. member for Churchill made reference to confrontation. That means the Liberal party decides that it has more to gain from confrontation than it has from co-operation. There is no bona fide attempt on the part of this government to sit down and negotiate a fair price and agreement with all of the producing provinces. There are some heroes in the cabinet. They have no desire to co-operate or conciliate. They make a lot of the fact that during the last election campaign they promised lower energy costs. But election promises have never bothered them in the past, so why should they bother them now? Nevertheless, these people are risking our country.
I want to deal with some of the comments made earlier in this debate, especially those made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). The minister stated that: "I think it is time that members of this House, and Canadians in general, grew up with respect to Canada's role in international affairs." The statement that every other country in the world would give their right arms to have a prime minister like the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) is one which I find completely incomprehensible. I suggest that Canada is already giving its right arm because of this Prime Minister. The problem is we are giving it to Saudi Arabia, Venezuela and Mexico. Perhaps it is about time the government appreciated the domestic situation in this country. Perhaps it is about time the government had more respect for Canada's ambitions than for the people of Saudi Arabia. If the government members really did appreciate our domestic situation, we would not be engaged in this debate. The Prime Minister does not want to stay here and face reality. The government has failed to reach a pricing agreement.

subtopic: PARKS CANADA-DECISION TO CANCEL CORNWALL TO PETERBOROUGH MOVE
PARKS CANADA-DECISION TO CANCEL CORNWALL TO PETERBOROUGH MOVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to spend some time tonight discussing certain of the comments made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Simmons). In an announcement to cancel the Parks Canada move from Cornwall to Peterborough, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) claimed, with lofty and saintly tones of compassion that his concerns are with the interests and morale of the majority of Parks Canada employees in Cornwall, especially the support staff who are less mobile and generally have fewer alternative work opportunities. Let me point out to this House that as of tonight there are over 20 unsettled claims before Treasury Board brought by the employees of the Parks Canada regional office in the city of Cornwall as a result of the cancellation of that move.
5080

November 25, 1980
Adjournment Debate
Leaving aside for the moment that 115 of the 145 employees of the Cornwall office went on record as being in favour of the move of the office to Peterborough, I take great exception to the sanctimonious appeal that the minister in cancelling the move is acting principally in the best interests of the employees of the Parks Canada regional office.
It is more than passing strange that this one small move of a regional office with no more than 150 employees was cancelled on the strength of employee morale. The reasons given in the Liberal policy announcements for the centralization were, first, to move the administration of federal government programs closer to the people directly affected by them and, second, to assist areas of slow economic development and high unemployment.
A 1978 Parks Canada document states, and 1 quote:
-average unemployment in the Peterborough area during 1977 was estimated at about 10 per cent of the labour force compared with ... 7 per cent in Ontario.
I might add that October, 1980, figures from the local employment office in Peterborough indicate that there has been a 33 per cent increase in unemployment there in the last 12 months. This compares to a less than one per cent increase nationally. With regard to the second point of the government's decentralization policy, that of economic development, the document states:
Peterborough's current economic difficulties are directly related to major layoffs and shutdowns . . . overall. The Peterborough area cannot continue to depend on its long established manufacturing industries for the steady supply of new jobs required by its expanding labour force.
Finally, with regard to the contention that a proposed move brings programs closer to the people affected by them, I would cite the following from an ADM in Parks Canada to the minister dated July 3, 1979. This document stated in part:
In 1974, a study of the implications of operating from Cornwall showed that inordinate transportation costs were involved in operating the region (as a whole). The essential close working relationships and co-ordination with the Ontario regional operation was seriously inhibited by the office location ... (In 1978) due to changed economic conditions, it was decided that Peterborough was now the best choice of location.
1 hope I do not weary members opposite with my unrelenting reiteration of the true facts of this case. But I digress for a moment. The minister was concerned with the welfare of the staff. I would like to point out that if the welfare of the staff is his major concern, what about the move of the staff of veterans affairs to other parts of Canada; what about the Liberal government's agonizing over the morale of the employees in Supply and Services when they moved to Shed-iac, New Brunswick, in the riding of the present Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc)? Did they squirm in mealy-mouthed Liberal platitudes voicing their compassion toward all the employees affected by moves which benefited no fewer than six Liberal cabinet ministers after federal relocation from Ottawa?
I suggest the reasons given by the Minister of the Environment on May 5, 1980, for cancelling the move of Parks Canada from Cornwall to Peterborough were nothing less than
hypocritical hogwash designed to camouflage this unmitigated piece of pork-barrelling, this clear case of patronage, this varnished example of cabinet level double dealing to satisfy rashly made election promises on the part of the present Minister of State for Trade, the minister from Cornwall (Mr. Lumley).
I would like to take this opportunity to make a certain sequence of events in this issue very clear. On August 3, 1979, I announced, and I quote, that "The Ontario regional office of Parks Canada will be moved to Peterborough during the summer of 1980". This was obviously not, as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment was pleased to put it in this House on May 12, 1980, an "announcement to defer". It was an announcement to inaugurate the proposal. The member for Burin-St. George's is simply factitious, adulterated and pettifogging and mendacious to suggest otherwise.
I suggest that I have not yet been satisfied on this point by the hon. member opposite. I would also ask that he fulfil the promise he made in this House on May 13 to produce documentation to support his claim, and to support the Minister of the Environment's contention that the minister "did not overlook the question of costs and the effects on the Parks Canada administration" in deciding to cancel the move.
I have in my hand an authority to enter into a lease in Peterborough, file No. 1020-P22/38, issued by Treasury Board on behalf of Public Works Canada, dated January 18, 1980. This document states:
It is estimated that the rental rate for the space now occupied by the client in Cornwall would increase to approximately $270,000 for fiscal year 1980-81, should the client continue to occupy this space.
In the absence of any convincing evidence to the contrary these figures stand as an indictment of this government's shameful, unforgivable and manipulative disregard for anyone or anything which does not relate directly to their own revolting self-interest.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: PARKS CANADA-DECISION TO CANCEL CORNWALL TO PETERBOROUGH MOVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the move from Cornwall to Peterborough was cancelled. It was cancelled on May 5, and I really would suggest to my good friend for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) that he get that message clear. It is cancelled. It is done. I said that to him last week. If I have to say it next week, I will be pleased to do so, until he gets the message that there is no mileage in this for him. We are aware, as he says, that not everyone was happy with the proposed move or with the decision to cancel. How many times does he want the careers of those people in limbo? The fact is, Mr. Speaker, the move is cancelled, it is done with and is not up for reconsideration.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts), acting in his capacity as minister responsible for Parks Canada, made the decision and announced it publicly on May 5 of this year.
November 25, 1980

The hon. member for Peterborough and I differ on what it was he, the hon. member for Peterborough, said in August of last year. He says that when he announced in August that something would take place the following year, that was an announcement to go ahead. I say that that was an announcement to delay a further year. He is not going to convince me, and I doubt whether 1 will convince him, so I suggest to him that we just leave it at a healthy difference of opinion.
As to the promise I am alleged to have made to this House, as I said to the hon. member last week, I made no commitment to him. I made a commitment to Madam Speaker to assist her in expediting the matter, as I knew she would. She did expedite it without my assistance, and I saw then and see now no need to pursue the matter any further.
At the same time, if the House feels that the document ought to be tabled, I would would be very glad to do so. There is nothing mischievous about the document at all, but I do think at some point, in fairness to the people of Peterborough and Cornwall and particularly to the Parks Canada employees involved, the hon. member should stop fighting yesterday's battles.
Surely the people of Peterborough riding sent the hon. member here to deal with more than one issue. I appeal to him to honour the mandate he has been given and to get on with some other more productive things such as tomorrow's issues and today's issues instead of yesterday's issues.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-LACK OF COVERAGE OF EUROPEAN CONFERENCE
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-LACK OF COVERAGE OF EUROPEAN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday, November 24, I asked a question of the Secretary of State and Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) about why the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, a Crown corporation, did not give adequate coverage to the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe presently being held in Madrid. This conference is the second follow-up meeting to discuss the implementation of the Helsinki Final Act of 1975. The First such meeting was held at Belgrade at the end of 1977 and during the early months of 1978.
The Madrid conference, as it has now become known, is expected to last through to the end of March, 1981. The Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe is focusing on three major themes or "baskets".
Basket 1 deals with respect for human rights and other principles of the Final Act: disarmament, arms control proposals, military confidence-building measures and military build-up in Europe.
Basket 2 deals with economic co-operation. This includes imports and exports, protectionism, transportation, energy and scientific research.
Adjournment Debate
Basket 3, which is of great importance to Canadians, covers such topics as family reunification, family visits, free flow of information and cultural exchanges.
The Helsinki conference in 1975 adopted ten principles which would guide relations between participating states. The ten principles adopted are as follows: First, sovereign equality, respect for the rights inherent in sovereignty; second, refraining from the threat or use of force; third, inviolability of frontiers; fourth, territorial integrity of states; fifth, peaceful settlement of disputes; sixth, non-intervention in internal affairs; seventh, respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, including freedom of thought, conscience, religion or belief; eighth, equal rights and self-determination of peoples; ninth, co-operation among states; and tenth, fulfilment in good faith of obligations under international law.
The Final Act states, and 1 quote:
All the principles set forth above are of primary significance and, accordingly, they will be equally and unreservedly applied, each of them being interpreted taking into account the others. The participating states express their determination fully to respect and apply these principles-
One of the goals of the Madrid conference is to analyse how far signatories of the Final Act have gone in implementing the provisions of the Final Act and to examine the progress which has been made in achieving the objectives of Helsinki.
Canada's Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Mac-Guigan) at the opening session of the Madrid follow-up meeting of the Conference on Security and Co-operation on November 12, 1980, was one of the first speakers to address the delegates from the 35 participating countries. The minister said that over the past five years we have seen important developments in co-operation between participating states through economic, scientific, cultural and other exchanges. The world is a better place for the conclusion of the Helsinki Final Act, 1975. There has been a recognition, with all due respect to national sovereignty, that no state is an island unto itself, able to conduct its affairs, either internal or external, in complete disregard for its neighbours.
The minister went on to say that the Final Act is designed to reduce tensions and to increase co-operation in Europe. In reviewing the implementations of the provisions of the Final Act, the Secretary of State for External Affairs said the following:
The deterioration in east-west relations, culminating last December in the Soviet intervention in Afghanistan, cannot be ignored in this forum . . . Soviet actions have challenged directly the principles in the Final Act of sovereign equality, refraining from the threat or use of force, inviolability of frontiers, the territorial integrity of states, non-intervention in internal affairs, and equal rights and self-determination of all peoples.
The minister went on to say that the alternative to detente is armed conflict. The shadow of Afghanistan will inevitably chill detente as long as Soviet troops remain there.
Under the human rights basket, the minister noted with great sadness that since the Final Act was signed people have been harassed, arrested, tried, exiled and imprisoned simply for trying to monitor and exercise their rights endorsed in the

November 25, 1980
Adjournment Debate
act. This persecution is inevitably a cause of friction in east-west relations today. The minister proposed a CSCE experts' meeting or some high level meeting to discuss the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms which are reaffirmed in principle No. 7 of the Final Act and the application of those rights in basket No. 3 dealing particularly with the question of the freer movement of people among participating states.
I have made the preceding remarks to indicate to Canadians the importance of the CSCE conference being held presently in Madrid and my great disappointment that our own Crown corporation, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, did not see fit to send even one reporter to cover this conference.
In reply to my question and concern, the Secretary of State and Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) answered in this House that the CBC entered into an agreement with Visnews which is a European news-gathering agency. Mr. Speaker, Canadians want to hear a Canadian viewpoint of this conference, not a European one.
Canadians are fed up with getting news secondhand, either through American or European news-collecting agencies. When taxpayers pay the money they do to have a publicly owned media, they expect better service than what they have been getting to date. I again put my question to the Minister of Communications: what steps does he propose to take to ensure that the remainder of the conference will get better coverage than it has received in the first two weeks of its deliberations?

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Simmons (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-LACK OF COVERAGE OF EUROPEAN CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Secretary of State and Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) and his parliamentary secretary, who are unavoidably absent tonight, I should like to respond to the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis). I thank him for bringing this matter to the attention of the House. He is quite right in stressing the importance of the Madrid conference which is being watched with interest throughout the world. It is to my friend's credit that he raised the issue at this time.
I do not think I need to remind members of the House of the arm's length relationship between the government and the CBC. While the Minister of Communications reports to Parliament for the CBC, he does not interfere in the day to day management of the corporation. I am sure all members are in agreement with this policy, especially in the area of news services.
However, as the minister undertook in the House yesterday, this question has been pursued with the CBC management. In response to the minister's inquiries, the CBC examined its coverage of the conference and informed the minister as follows. As far as English television is concerned, the decision was made not to assign a reporter to Madrid for two reasons. The first was that all the coverage which would be needed was available to the CBC through Visnews, the world's foremost agency in the field of television news. By the way, the CBC is a founding member of Visnews which was formed by a number
of broadcasting agencies specifically to provide television coverage of international news events. In this way individual broadcaster's resources are not stretched by having to assign reporters or film crews to an event which is already fully covered. Visnews provides pooled coverage of the conference which is available to all its member organizations. Within that context it was felt by CBC that as the conference lasts for many weeks, and no one could be spared for that length of time, the Visnews service would be adequate for network purposes.
During the first week of the conference in Madrid, "The National" carried four stories, first a scene-setter from Mark Phillips in London using film footage from Visnews and Eurovision of the delegates gathering. For three successive evenings after this, "The National" carried footage by satellite from Europe and voice-over reports from speeches by the Secretary of State (Mr. MacGuigan) and the chief delegates from the United States and the Soviet Union. The English television service is monitoring the work of the conference closely with the help of its London bureau and will resume the story as warranted by events.
On English radio 19 separate items on the conference were carried on network newscasts between November 10 and 16. There is no CBC reporter in attendance but reports have been taken from the BBC, NBC and freelancers. English radio's current affairs section carried interviews about the conference on "As it Happens" and "Sunday Morning." Also, commentary on the meeting featured Jim Cutler, law professor at McGill University and lawyer for Soviet dissidents.
Coverage on the French services is being greatly hampered by the strike of their journalists in Quebec, but the radio service has, as well as carrying a pre-conference item, included in its information programs a number of items about the conference.
Mr. Speaker, the conference has a long way to go. The CBC feels its news staff must exercise judgment in deciding which parts of the proceedings to report. The hon. member for Parkdale-High Park can be assured that his comments tonight will be noted by CBC management and the Minister of Communications will make a point of bringing them to the attention of the president of the CBC.
In conclusion, on behalf of the minister, I would like to thank the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park for raising this important issue.

SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT-RENEWAL OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FUNDING-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks tonight deal with the question I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) on November 4 about the meaning of the words in the second last paragraph on page 13 of the budget paper in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) claims that he expects significant
November 25, 1980

savings to come out of the upcoming renewal of federal-provincial funding arrangements for health and social development. I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare where she expected the savings to come from. Mr. Speaker, instead of receiving an answer I received the usual lecture, plus a vague indication-and I quote:
-the savings to come as a result of discussions with those provinces which presently have a surplus-
This evening I ask: what does this mean? Does it mean there is to be a continuation of block funding for medicare, with a reduction of federal contributions to block funding? Likewise, are the provinces being expected to pick up a higher percentage of the established programs themselves with the federal government moving in, perhaps as Justice Hall recommended, to cost-share with the poorer provinces in order to maintain a comprehensive health care system? Is this the intent of the minister? This may sound good superficially but I think caution is in order since it further erodes federal ability to enforce national health care standards. It presupposes that richer provinces have better programs, which is false. It is in the three richest provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario that we find phenomena like premiums and extra billing, evidence that the quality of health care in any particular province is as much a matter of philosophy as it is a matter of wealth. The minister needs to tell us more. The Canadian public deserves to know more about what she intends for health care funding in Canada. Because the Hall report has been released, she can no longer hide behind the fact that it has yet to be released. Instead, we find her hiding behind the idea of federal-provincial consultation. She cannot give anything away because she is embroiled in this process of consultation. I ask this evening, Mr. Speaker, what happened to the great defender of medicare who we heard so much about during the time the Liberals were in opposition?
On that same day the minister indicated she would not turn to block funding for social services. We are glad to hear that. We welcome that announcement on her part since we feel that block funding has not been a success where it has been applied, particularly with regard to medicare. Unfortunately, she is also reported to have said, outside the House on the same day, that post-secondary education, another aspect of established program-financing, might be an area where savings could be made. The minister was quoted in the papers as saying that post-secondary education was an area where savings could be made because it was elitist. Does this mean she thinks postsecondary education should be elitist? If the federal government pulls out of this area and reduces its commitment to it post-secondary education will become elitist in this country.
There is a trend toward a renewed elitism in post-secondary education. I hope the minister will try to fight this trend and not give in or use it as an excuse to save money at the expense
Adjournment Debate
of equality of opportunity. It is time we heard from the minister personally, if not tonight, then on some other occasion, as to just what she meant when she indicated that in her view post-secondary education was elitist and therefore an avenue which the government might use in the upcoming renewal of federal-provincial funding arrangements for established programs.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Frith (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the Senate
subtopic: SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT-RENEWAL OF FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FUNDING-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by addressing the second part of the question raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie). The hon. member has consistently made allegations in the House with respect to the minister's commitment to medicare and the government's response to the recommendations of the Hall report. The minister has pointed out in the House on previous occasions that the government is spending $7.1 billion on medicare. We have also pointed out that the increased commitment of the federal government with respect to the established program funding laid out in 1977 has enabled the provinces to use those additional funds to expand into the field of extended health care. As a result of this increased federal spending, the provinces, with the exception of Alberta and Ontario, have been able to, for example, extend denticare to children and intermediate nursing home care to the elderly. These are the areas of growth with respect to medicare.
As a result of the policies developed by the minister and the government these programs have been implemented. Many of the remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill and other hon. members opposite have led the public to believe that the government intends to decrease the amount of money to be spent on social development in Canada. It has been pointed out by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on several occasions in the House that this is simply not the case. It is a basic priority of this government to cover those groups in our society which it has traditionally supported in terms of our priorities and our principles. I refer to the elderly, the sick, the oppressed and the underprivileged.
I think our expenditures in these areas indicate that we have been true to our commitment and our philosophy. Over the past ten years expenditures in the social development envelope have increased by 300 per cent. In the coming year there will be an increase in the total amount spent on social development in Canada. The government is still committed to those basic priorities which have traditionally been part of its philosophy, and we have no intention, as the hon. member has mentioned, of going to block funding for social development.
